questions.why: The bulbourethral glands are also called Cowper's glands. They are pea-sized glands below the prostate that release a clear, alkaline mucus into the spongy urethra. The mucus lubricates the urethra and neutralizes traces of urine before sperm pass through.
notes: Bartholin's glands are the greater vestibular glands of the female, which lubricate the vestibule beside the vaginal opening. Pick them if the question asked for the female counterpart of the bulbourethral glands.
Leydig cells are the interstitial cells of the testis that produce testosterone. They are cells between the seminiferous tubules, not a gland that empties into the urethra.
Skene's glands are small female glands that open near the external urethral orifice, also called the paraurethral glands. Choose them if the question asked about glands beside the female urethra.
Correct. Cowper's glands is another name for the bulbourethral glands.

questions.q: How many columns of erectile tissue does the penis contain?
questions.why: The penis is built around three columns of erectile tissue. Two are the corpora cavernosa, which run along the dorsal side, and one is the corpus spongiosum, which runs along the ventral side and surrounds the spongy urethra. All three fill with blood during an erection.
notes: Two counts only the paired corpora cavernosa and leaves out the single corpus spongiosum. Students who remember only the two larger columns pick this.
Correct. Two corpora cavernosa plus one corpus spongiosum make three.
Four comes from counting the corpus spongiosum twice, once for its column and once for the glans at its tip. The glans is an expansion of the spongiosum, not a separate column.
One counts only the corpus spongiosum around the urethra and leaves out the two corpora cavernosa. Students who remember only the column with the urethra tend to pick this.

questions.q: Which column of erectile tissue surrounds the spongy urethra?
questions.why: The corpus spongiosum is the single ventral column of erectile tissue, and it surrounds the urethra along the full length of the penis. That is why this part of the urethra is named the spongy urethra. The corpus spongiosum ends at the tip by expanding into the glans penis.
notes: The prepuce is the fold of skin over the glans, not erectile tissue. It would be the answer if the question asked what the foreskin is called.

The crura are the anchored ends of the corpora cavernosa in the root of the penis, and they do not hold the urethra. Choose them if the question asked how the dorsal columns attach to the pelvic bones.
Correct. The corpus spongiosum surrounds the spongy urethra.
The corpora cavernosa are the two dorsal columns, and the urethra does not run through them. Pick them if the question asked which paired columns run along the dorsal side.

questions.q: Sperm leave the testis. Which duct of the male duct system do they enter first?
questions.why: The epididymis is the first duct of the male duct system, sitting right on the back of the testis. Sperm enter it from the testis, are stored there, and gain the ability to move. From the epididymis, the route continues into the ductus deferens, then the ejaculatory duct, and finally the urethra.
notes: The ejaculatory duct comes after the ductus deferens, deep in the pelvis. Choose it if the question asked which duct the ductus deferens helps form.
The ductus deferens comes after the epididymis, beginning at its tail. Pick it if the question asked which duct sperm enter after the epididymis.
Correct. The epididymis is the first duct sperm enter after leaving the testis.
The urethra is the last duct on the route, the shared tube to the outside. It would be the answer if the question asked which duct sperm pass through just before leaving the body.

questions.q: Where along the male duct system does seminal vesicle fluid first mix with the sperm?
questions.why: The duct of each seminal vesicle joins the ampulla of the ductus deferens, and the two together form the ejaculatory duct. So the ejaculatory duct is the first place where sperm and seminal vesicle fluid flow together. The mixture then enters the prostatic urethra, where prostate fluid is added.
notes: Correct. Seminal vesicle fluid first meets the sperm in the ejaculatory duct.
The epididymis stores sperm on the back of the testis, long before any gland fluid is added. Pick it if the question asked where sperm are stored and mature.
The ductus deferens carries only sperm until its end, where the seminal vesicle duct joins it. Choose it if the question asked which duct carries sperm through the inguinal canal.
The spongy urethra is where the bulbourethral glands add their mucus, much later on the route. It would be the answer if the question asked where bulbourethral mucus enters.

questions.q: Which cells line the seminiferous tubules and form the blood-testis barrier?
questions.why: The sustentacular cells, also called Sertoli cells, line the seminiferous tubules and surround the developing sperm. Tight connections between neighboring Sertoli cells form the blood-testis barrier, which separates the developing sperm from the blood supply. They also nourish the sperm as they develop.
notes: The interstitial (Leydig) cells sit between the tubules and produce testosterone. Pick them if the question asked which cells of the testis make the male hormone.

Juxtaglomerular cells are modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole of the kidney, part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus. They would be the answer if the question asked about the JGA.
Correct. Sustentacular cells line the tubules and form the blood-testis barrier.

Podocytes are kidney cells that wrap around the glomerular capillaries and form part of the filtration membrane, a different barrier in a different organ. Choose them if the question asked about the filtration membrane of the kidney.

questions.q: Starting at the bladder, which order correctly lists the three regions of the male urethra?
questions.why: The male urethra first passes through the prostate just below the bladder (the prostatic urethra). It then crosses the floor of the pelvis in the perineum as the short membranous urethra. Finally, it runs the length of the penis inside the corpus spongiosum as the spongy urethra, the longest region.
notes: This puts the membranous region first, but the prostate sits directly against the bladder, so the prostatic urethra must come first.
This order begins in the penis and ends in the pelvic floor, which mixes the outermost region with the deep ones. The spongy urethra is the last region, not the first.
Correct. Prostatic, then membranous, then spongy.
This swaps the last two. The membranous urethra is the short middle stretch through the pelvic floor, and the spongy urethra comes after it in the penis.

questions.q: Which gland adds a milky fluid that helps sperm stay active?
questions.why: The prostate is the single gland below the bladder that surrounds the urethra. Many small ducts carry its milky fluid into the prostatic urethra, where it helps the sperm stay active. The seminal vesicles and the bulbourethral glands, in contrast, add alkaline secretions.
notes: The seminal vesicles add an alkaline fluid rich in fructose, the largest share of semen. Pick them if the question asked which gland supplies the sugar sperm use for energy.
The testes make sperm and testosterone, not the fluid portion of semen. They would be the answer if the question asked which organs are the male gonads.
Correct. The prostate adds a milky fluid that helps sperm stay active.
The bulbourethral glands add a clear, alkaline mucus. Choose them if the question asked which glands lubricate the urethra and neutralize urine.

questions.q: Which serous membrane, derived from the peritoneum, partly covers each testis?
questions.why: The tunica vaginalis is a serous membrane that came from a pouch of peritoneum carried down with the testis as it descended. It partly covers the front and sides of each testis, outside the tunica albuginea. Like other serous membranes, it has two layers with a thin film of fluid between them, and too much fluid here is called a hydrocele.
notes: The visceral pleura is the serous membrane on the surface of each lung. Choose it if the question asked which membrane covers the lungs.
Correct. The tunica vaginalis is the serous membrane around the testis.

The parietal peritoneum lines the wall of the abdominopelvic cavity. The tunica vaginalis is derived from it, but the parietal peritoneum itself stays in the abdomen, so pick it only if the question asked what lines the abdominal wall.
The tunica albuginea is the fibrous capsule of the testis, deep to the tunica vaginalis, and it is not a serous membrane. Pick it if the question asked which capsule divides the testis into lobules.

questions.q: Which part of the penis contains the bulb and the crura?
questions.why: The root is the attached portion of the penis in the perineum. It contains the bulb, the enlarged base of the corpus spongiosum, and the two crura, the anchored ends of the corpora cavernosa that attach to the pelvic bones. These anchor the penis, while the body and glans hang free.
notes: Correct. The root contains the bulb and the crura.
The body is the free, movable shaft, where the three erectile columns run side by side. Pick it if the question asked for the part between the root and the tip.
The glans is the acorn-shaped tip, the expansion of the corpus spongiosum at the opposite end from the bulb. Choose it if the question asked which part the external urethral orifice opens on.
The prepuce is the foreskin over the glans, a fold of skin with no erectile columns. It would be the answer if the question asked what is removed in circumcision.

questions.q: The tunica albuginea sends walls inward into each testis. What does it divide the testis into?
questions.why: The tunica albuginea is the white fibrous capsule of the testis. Walls of this capsule extend inward and divide the testis into a few hundred small, wedge-shaped lobules. Each lobule holds tightly coiled seminiferous tubules, where sperm are made.
notes: Correct. The tunica albuginea divides each testis into a few hundred lobules.
Three erectile columns describe the penis, with two corpora cavernosa and one corpus spongiosum. Choose this if the question asked how the erectile tissue of the penis is arranged.
Root, body, and glans are the three regions of the penis. They would be the answer if the question asked how the penis is divided from base to tip.
Right and left compartments are made by the scrotal septum, which divides the scrotum, not the testis. Pick this if the question asked what the scrotal septum does.

questions.q: Which structure is removed in a circumcision?
questions.why: Circumcision removes the prepuce, the loose fold of skin, also called the foreskin, that covers the glans penis. The glans and the erectile columns beneath it are left intact. After circumcision, the glans is exposed rather than covered.
notes: The raphe is the seam-like ridge on the surface of the scrotum. Choose it if the question asked what marks the midline of the scrotum.
Correct. Circumcision removes the prepuce.
The glans is the acorn-shaped tip that the prepuce covers, and it stays in place after circumcision. Pick it if the question asked for the expanded end of the corpus spongiosum.

The corpus spongiosum is the erectile column around the urethra, deep to the skin, and it is not touched in circumcision. It would be the answer if the question asked which column surrounds the spongy urethra.

questions.q: Which region of the male urethra runs through the penis inside the corpus spongiosum?
questions.why: The spongy urethra, also called the penile urethra, runs through the penis inside the corpus spongiosum, which is how it gets its name. It is the longest of the three regions and ends at the external urethral orifice on the glans. The bulbourethral glands release their mucus into it.
notes: Correct. The spongy urethra runs inside the corpus spongiosum.

The ejaculatory duct is not part of the urethra; it is the short duct that empties into the prostatic urethra. It would be the answer if the question asked which duct the ductus deferens and seminal vesicle duct form.

The membranous urethra is the short middle region crossing the floor of the pelvis, between the prostate and the penis. Choose it if the question asked which region lies beside the bulbourethral glands.
The prostatic urethra is the first region, running through the prostate just below the bladder. Pick it if the question asked where the ejaculatory ducts empty.

questions.q: In cryptorchidism, an undescended testis stays at core body temperature. Which cells are at risk if it is not corrected?
options: The erectile tissue of the penis
The mucus glands beside the urethra
The sperm-forming cells of the testis
The fluid-secreting cells of the prostate
questions.why: Sperm production needs a temperature a few degrees below the body core, which is why the testes normally hang in the scrotum. An undescended testis stays inside at core body temperature, and if the problem is not corrected, the warmth can damage the cells that form sperm. The problem is local to the testis that did not descend.
notes: The erectile tissue of the penis is not affected by where the testis sits. Choose it if the question asked what fills with blood during an erection.
The bulbourethral glands beside the urethra are pelvic glands that normally sit at body temperature. They would be the answer if the question asked which glands secrete alkaline mucus.
Correct. The warmth threatens the sperm-forming cells in the undescended testis.
The prostate is deep in the pelvis at body temperature already and works normally there. Pick it if the question asked which gland is enlarged in benign prostatic hyperplasia.
questions.answerText: The sperm-forming cells of the testis

questions.q: An older man's enlarged prostate makes urination difficult. Which tube is the prostate squeezing?
questions.why: The male urethra passes straight through the prostate just below the bladder. When the prostate enlarges, it presses inward on this part of the urethra and narrows it, so urine has trouble flowing out. That is how a reproductive gland causes a urinary symptom.
notes: The ureters carry urine from the kidneys and enter the back of the bladder above the prostate, so the prostate does not surround them. Pick ureter if the question asked which tubes drain the kidneys.
The ductus deferens carries sperm, not urine, and it ends behind the bladder before reaching the prostate. Choose it if the question asked which duct is cut in a vasectomy.
Correct. The enlarged prostate squeezes the urethra that runs through it.

The ejaculatory ducts do pass through the prostate, but they carry sperm and seminal fluid, not urine, so squeezing them would not make urination difficult. They would be the answer if the question asked which ducts empty into the prostatic urethra.

questions.q: Which disorder is an abnormal swelling of the veins that drain the testis?
questions.why: A varicocele is an abnormal swelling of the veins that drain the testis, the pampiniform plexus in the spermatic cord. The name links varic-, as in varicose veins, with -cele, meaning swelling. It is the vein disorder of the scrotum, while a hydrocele is the fluid disorder.
notes: An inguinal hernia is a loop of intestine pushing through the inguinal canal. It would be the answer if the question described intestine bulging in the groin.
A hydrocele is a collection of serous fluid in the tunica vaginalis around the testis, not a vein problem. Pick it if the question described a fluid-filled swelling.
Correct. A varicocele is swelling of the veins that drain the testis.
Cryptorchidism is the failure of a testis to descend into the scrotum. Choose it if the question described a testis that stayed in the abdomen.

questions.q: A man's prostate is enlarged and squeezing his urethra, but a biopsy shows no cancer. What is this condition called?
questions.why: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate. Benign means not cancer, and hyperplasia means growth from an increase in the number of cells. Because the prostate surrounds the urethra, the enlarged gland squeezes it and makes urination difficult.
notes: A varicocele is a swelling of the veins that drain the testis, nowhere near the urethra. Choose it if the question described enlarged veins in the scrotum.
Correct. A non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate is benign prostatic hyperplasia.
Prostate cancer is a malignant tumor of the prostate. The biopsy showed no cancer, so this does not fit, but pick it if the question described a malignant growth of the prostate.
A hydrocele is serous fluid collecting in the tunica vaginalis around a testis. It would be the answer if the question described a fluid-filled swelling in the scrotum.

questions.q: Serous fluid collects in the tunica vaginalis around one testis. Which disorder is this?
questions.why: A hydrocele is a collection of serous fluid in the tunica vaginalis, the serous membrane around the testis. The name combines hydro-, meaning water, with -cele, meaning swelling. Normally only a thin film of fluid sits between the two layers of the tunica vaginalis, so extra fluid makes the scrotum swell.
notes: An inguinal hernia is a loop of intestine pushing through the inguinal canal. It would be the answer if the question described intestine bulging in the groin.
Correct. Fluid in the tunica vaginalis is a hydrocele.
A varicocele is a swelling of the veins that drain the testis, not a collection of fluid. Pick it if the question described enlarged veins in the scrotum.
Cryptorchidism is a testis that never descended into the scrotum. Choose it if the question described a testis that stayed in the abdomen.

questions.q: The testes hang in the scrotum, outside the main body cavity. Why is this outside position important?
options: The scrotum shields the testes better than the abdomen does
Sperm production needs a temperature above core body temperature
The testes are too large to fit inside the pelvic cavity
Sperm production needs a temperature below core body temperature
questions.why: Sperm form properly only at a temperature a few degrees below the body core of 37°C (98.6°F). Hanging the testes in the scrotum keeps them cooler than they would be in the abdomen. The cremaster and dartos muscles fine-tune that temperature by moving the testes and tightening the scrotal skin.
notes: The scrotum actually offers less protection than the bony pelvis or muscular abdomen, which is why the testes are vulnerable to injury. The outside position is a trade-off made for temperature, not safety.
This reverses the requirement. Sperm need cooler conditions, not warmer ones, which is why an undescended testis at body temperature can have its sperm-forming cells damaged.
Size is not the reason; the testes would fit in the pelvis, and organs of similar size sit there. This is a guess at a cause, while the real reason for the outside position is temperature.
Correct. The scrotum keeps the testes cooler than the core, which sperm production needs.
questions.answerText: Sperm production needs a temperature below core body temperature

questions.q: The seminiferous tubules are very long and tightly coiled inside each testis. Why is this coiled design useful?
options: Coiling keeps the tubules warmer than the rest of the body
Coiling packs a long sperm-making tube into a small space
Coiling lets the tubules secrete most of the fluid in semen
Coiling stores sperm until they gain the ability to swim
questions.why: The testes produce huge numbers of sperm, and that takes a great deal of sperm-forming tissue. Coiling very long tubules tightly inside the lobules fits an enormous total length of tubule, and the lining that makes sperm, into a small organ. This is the same idea as the folds and coils seen in other organs that need a lot of working surface in a small space.
notes: Sperm production needs cooler conditions, not warmer ones, so making the tubules warmer would harm them. Students who mix up the temperature rule tend to choose this.
Correct. Coiling fits a great length of sperm-producing tubule into the small testis.
Most of the fluid in semen comes from the seminal vesicles, not the seminiferous tubules. This would fit a question about the seminal vesicles, which supply the largest share of semen.
Storing sperm until they can swim is the job of the epididymis, the coiled duct on the back of the testis. Pick this if the question asked why the epididymis is needed.
questions.answerText: Coiling packs a long sperm-making tube into a small space

questions.q: Sperm collected directly from the seminiferous tubules are fully formed but cannot swim. Which step have they not yet gone through?
options: Receiving fructose from the seminal vesicles
questions.why: Sperm leave the seminiferous tubules with all their parts, but they gain the ability to move only after time in the epididymis. The epididymis stores them while they mature, so a reserve of motile sperm is ready at ejaculation. Sperm taken straight from the tubules have skipped this step.
notes: Correct. Sperm gain motility while maturing in the epididymis.

The ejaculatory duct is a passageway near the end of the route; passing through it does not give sperm the ability to swim. Choose it if the question asked where seminal vesicle fluid first joins the sperm.

Fructose fuels swimming, but sperm must first be able to swim, which they gain in the epididymis before they ever meet seminal vesicle fluid. This would fit a question about where sperm get their energy.
Prostate fluid helps sperm stay active, but it is added later in the prostatic urethra, after sperm can already move. Pick this if the question asked what the prostate contributes.

questions.q: Seminal vesicle fluid is rich in fructose. What does the fructose do for sperm?
options: It neutralizes acidic urine in the urethra
It gives sperm the energy to swim
It helps the sperm penetrate the oocyte
questions.why: Fructose is a sugar, and sperm use it as fuel for the whipping movement of the tail. The seminal vesicles supply this fuel in an alkaline fluid that also gives the sperm a liquid to swim in. This nourishment helps the sperm keep swimming on the long trip toward the oocyte.
notes: Neutralizing acidic urine in the urethra is the job of the alkaline mucus from the bulbourethral glands. Pick this if the question asked what bulbourethral mucus does.
The blood-testis barrier is formed by tight connections between Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules, not by any gland fluid. Choose this if the question asked what the sustentacular cells do.
Correct. Fructose is the fuel sperm use to swim.
Getting through the coverings of the oocyte depends on enzymes in the acrosome, the cap on the sperm head. This would fit a question about the acrosome.
questions.answerText: It gives sperm the energy to swim

questions.q: A mature sperm has almost no cytoplasm and few parts besides a nucleus, mitochondria, and a tail. Which statement best explains how this design fits its job?
options: Removing cytoplasm lets the sperm divide again in the female tract
The acrosome replaces the mitochondria as the energy source
The tail carries the chromosomes, which keeps the head small
A light, streamlined cell swims fast on energy from its mitochondria
questions.why: A sperm's job is to deliver its chromosomes to the oocyte, which means swimming a long way. Shedding most of its cytoplasm keeps the cell small and light, the tail provides the swimming motion, and the mitochondria packed into the middle piece supply the energy. Every remaining part serves that trip.
notes: Sperm do not divide after they are formed; their job ends with fertilization. This statement treats the sperm like a body cell that can keep dividing, which is a misconception.
The acrosome holds enzymes for getting into the oocyte, not energy. Energy comes from the mitochondria of the middle piece, so pick the acrosome only if the question asked about penetrating the egg.
The chromosomes are in the nucleus in the head, not the tail. This mixes up the part that carries genetic material with the part that moves the cell.
Correct. A small, light cell with mitochondria powering its tail is built for fast travel.
questions.answerText: A light, streamlined cell swims fast on energy from its mitochondria

questions.q: On a cold day the testes are pulled up closer to the body, and on a warm day they hang lower. Why is this adjustment useful?
options: It keeps the testes at full core body temperature
It protects the testes from injury during movement
It keeps the testes near the cooler temperature sperm need
It moves sperm from the testes into the epididymis
questions.why: Sperm form best a few degrees below the body core, so the testes must stay slightly cool but not too cold. In the cold, the cremaster muscle pulls them toward the warm body, and in warm weather it relaxes so they hang lower and lose heat. The dartos helps by tightening or loosening the scrotal skin.
notes: Holding the testes at full core temperature would harm sperm production, which is the problem in an undescended testis. The adjustment aims for slightly below core temperature.

The scrotum does little to shield the testes from injury, and the warm and cold pattern in the question tracks temperature, not movement. This option guesses at a purpose the question does not describe.
Correct. Raising and lowering the testes keeps them near the cooler temperature sperm need.
Sperm move from the testis into the epididymis through ducts, not by raising or lowering the testes. This would only fit a question about the route sperm take after they form.
questions.answerText: It keeps the testes near the cooler temperature sperm need

questions.q: In benign prostatic hyperplasia, which region of the urethra is narrowed?
questions.why: The prostatic urethra is the first region of the male urethra, running straight through the prostate just below the bladder. When the prostate enlarges in benign prostatic hyperplasia, it presses inward on this region and narrows it. That is why the problem shows up as a weak or slow urine stream.
notes: Correct. The prostatic urethra runs through the prostate, so it is the region narrowed in BPH.
The spongy urethra runs through the penis inside the corpus spongiosum, far from the prostate. Choose it if the question asked which region is the longest.
The external urethral orifice is the opening at the tip of the glans. It would be the answer if the question asked where urine and semen leave the body.
The membranous urethra is the short region below the prostate crossing the floor of the pelvis, outside the gland. Pick it if the question asked which region the bulbourethral glands sit beside.

questions.q: Which organs are the male gonads, the organs that produce sperm and secrete hormones?
questions.why: The testes are the male gonads, the primary reproductive organs. Inside each testis, the seminiferous tubules produce sperm, and the interstitial cells between those tubules produce testosterone. Every other male reproductive structure either stores and carries the sperm or adds fluid to it.
notes: Each epididymis is a coiled duct on the back of a testis where sperm are stored and gain the ability to move. It does not make sperm; pick it if the question asked where sperm mature after they form.
The seminal vesicles are accessory glands that add an alkaline, fructose-rich fluid to semen. Choose them if the question asked which gland makes the largest share of the semen volume.
Correct. The testes produce sperm and secrete hormones such as testosterone.
These are accessory glands that add fluid to semen, not gonads. Pick them if the question asked which glands add milky fluid and lubricating mucus to the sperm.

questions.q: Which white fibrous capsule surrounds each testis and divides it into lobules?
questions.why: The tunica albuginea is a tough capsule of dense connective tissue wrapped tightly around each testis, and its name means white coat. Extensions of this capsule run inward and divide the testis into a few hundred lobules. Each lobule holds coiled seminiferous tubules, where sperm are produced.
notes: The scrotal septum divides the scrotum into two compartments, one for each testis. It separates the two testes rather than dividing a single testis; pick it if the question asked what splits the scrotal sac down the middle.
Correct. The tunica albuginea is the white capsule whose extensions divide the testis into lobules.

The dartos is the layer of smooth muscle in the scrotal skin that wrinkles the skin to reduce heat loss. It belongs to the scrotum, not the testis capsule; choose it if the question asked which muscle wrinkles the scrotum.
The tunica vaginalis is a serous membrane, derived from the peritoneum, that partly covers the testis outside the tunica albuginea. Pick it if the question asked where fluid collects in a hydrocele.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the sustentacular (Sertoli) cells and the interstitial (Leydig) cells of the testis?
options: Sertoli cells line the tubules and nourish sperm; Leydig cells lie between the tubules and make testosterone
Both cell types line the tubules, and both develop directly into mature sperm cells
Sertoli cells lie between the tubules and make testosterone; Leydig cells line the tubules and nourish sperm
Sertoli cells line the epididymis and store sperm; Leydig cells line the ductus deferens
questions.why: Sustentacular means supporting, and the Sertoli cells sit inside the walls of the seminiferous tubules, where they nourish developing sperm and form the blood-testis barrier. Interstitial means in between, and the Leydig cells sit in the connective tissue between the tubules, where they produce testosterone. The names describe where each cell lives.
notes: Correct. Sertoli cells support sperm inside the tubules, and Leydig cells make testosterone between them.
Only the Sertoli cells line the tubules, and neither cell type turns into sperm. Sperm develop from separate germ cells in the tubule wall, which the Sertoli cells surround and support.
This swaps the two cell types. Interstitial means in between, so the Leydig cells are the ones between the tubules; students choose this when they mix up the two people's names.

Both cell types are found in the testis, not in the ducts. Sperm storage happens in the epididymis, which would be the answer if the question asked where sperm wait and mature after leaving the testis.
questions.answerText: Sertoli cells line the tubules and nourish sperm; Leydig cells lie between the tubules and make testosterone

questions.q: Why do the testes sit in the scrotum, outside the abdominopelvic cavity?
options: Testosterone can only enter the blood from outside the body cavity
The scrotum shields the testes better than the bony pelvis could
Sperm production needs a temperature a few degrees below the body core
Sperm production needs a temperature a few degrees above the body core
questions.why: Sperm develop best at a temperature a few degrees below the body core temperature of 37°C (98.6°F). Hanging the testes in the scrotum keeps them cooler, and two muscles fine-tune that temperature: the cremaster raises or lowers the testes, and the dartos wrinkles the scrotal skin. When a testis fails to descend (cryptorchidism), the extra warmth can damage its sperm-forming cells if it is not corrected.
notes: Testosterone enters the blood just as well from inside the body, as shown by the ovaries, which make hormones while sitting in the pelvic cavity. The reason for the scrotal position is temperature, not hormone release.
The scrotum actually leaves the testes more exposed to injury than the bony pelvis would. This position is a trade-off accepted for temperature, not a form of protection.
Correct. The scrotum keeps the testes slightly cooler than the core, which sperm production requires.
This reverses the temperature. If warmth were needed, the testes would sit deep in the body; the cremaster pulls them closer to the body only when it is cold, to keep them from cooling too much.
questions.answerText: Sperm production needs a temperature a few degrees below the body core

questions.q: In which structure are sperm stored while they mature and gain the ability to swim?
questions.why: The epididymis is a comma-shaped, tightly coiled duct on the back of each testis. Sperm leave the seminiferous tubules unable to swim, and they gain motility while they are stored in the epididymis. From there they move into the ductus deferens when it is time to leave.
notes: The seminiferous tubules are where sperm are produced inside the testis. Sperm leave them before they can swim, so pick this if the question asked where sperm form.
The ductus deferens carries sperm from the epididymis up toward the urethra. It is the transport tube that comes next; choose it if the question asked which duct runs in the spermatic cord.
Correct. Sperm are stored in the epididymis and gain motility there.
The seminal vesicle is an accessory gland that adds fluid to semen, not a place where sperm mature. Pick it if the question asked which gland adds a fructose-rich fluid.

questions.q: Which duct carries sperm from the epididymis up out of the scrotum toward the urethra?
questions.why: The ductus deferens, also called the vas deferens, begins at the epididymis and runs up through the spermatic cord, through the inguinal canal, and into the pelvis. Behind the bladder it joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct. It is the long transport tube between storage in the epididymis and the urethra.
notes: The ejaculatory duct is the short duct formed where the ductus deferens meets the seminal vesicle duct, and it empties into the prostatic urethra. It is one step later; pick it if the question asked which duct passes through the prostate.
The spongy urethra runs through the penis and is the last stretch of the path to the outside. Pick it if the question asked which part of the urethra lies within the corpus spongiosum.

The spermatic cord is a bundle, not a duct. It wraps the ductus deferens together with blood vessels, nerves, and the cremaster muscle, so choose it if the question asked what bundle passes through the inguinal canal.
Correct. The ductus deferens carries sperm from the epididymis toward the urethra.

questions.q: Which structure is a bundle containing the ductus deferens, blood vessels, nerves, and the cremaster muscle?
questions.why: The spermatic cord is a bundle that runs from the scrotum up through the inguinal canal. It holds the ductus deferens together with the testicular artery and veins, nerves, and lymphatic vessels, all wrapped in layers that include the cremaster muscle. It is the lifeline that connects each testis to the body.
notes: The epididymis is a single coiled duct on the testis where sperm are stored. It is not a bundle of several structures; pick it if the question asked where sperm gain motility.
Correct. The spermatic cord bundles the ductus deferens with vessels, nerves, and the cremaster muscle.
The corpus spongiosum is the single column of erectile tissue in the penis that surrounds the spongy urethra. Pick it if the question asked which erectile column holds the urethra.

The tunica vaginalis is a serous membrane that partly covers the testis. It surrounds the testis rather than bundling vessels and ducts; choose it if the question asked which membrane fills with fluid in a hydrocele.

questions.q: How is the ejaculatory duct formed, and where does it empty?
options: The seminal vesicle joins the bulbourethral duct; it empties into the urinary bladder
The epididymis joins the ductus deferens inside the testis; it empties into the membranous urethra
The ductus deferens joins a prostatic duct; it empties into the spongy urethra of the penis
The ductus deferens joins the seminal vesicle duct; it empties into the prostatic urethra
questions.why: Behind the bladder, each ductus deferens merges with the duct of a seminal vesicle to form a short ejaculatory duct. The two ejaculatory ducts then pass into the prostate and empty into the prostatic urethra, the first part of the urethra. From there sperm travel through the membranous and spongy urethra to the outside.
notes: The bulbourethral glands sit below the prostate and drain into the spongy urethra, and nothing in the duct system empties into the bladder. Pick the bulbourethral glands if the question asked which glands release lubricating mucus into the urethra.

The epididymis connects to the ductus deferens back at the testis, not where the ejaculatory duct forms. The membranous urethra is the short segment after the prostate, so the location is also one step too far.
The prostate is not one of the ducts that forms the ejaculatory duct; the ejaculatory duct runs through the prostate. The spongy urethra is in the penis, too far along the path.
Correct. The ductus deferens and seminal vesicle duct merge, and the ejaculatory duct empties into the prostatic urethra.
questions.answerText: The ductus deferens joins the seminal vesicle duct; it empties into the prostatic urethra

questions.q: Which list traces sperm from where they are made to the outside of the body?
options: Seminiferous tubules, ductus deferens, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, urethra
Epididymis, seminiferous tubules, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra
Seminiferous tubules, epididymis, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra
Seminiferous tubules, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, ductus deferens, urethra
questions.why: Sperm are made only in the seminiferous tubules of the testis. They move into the epididymis to be stored and gain motility, then travel up the ductus deferens through the spermatic cord. The ductus deferens joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct, which empties into the urethra for the final trip out.
notes: This swaps the epididymis and the ductus deferens. Sperm reach the epididymis first, directly from the testis, and only then enter the ductus deferens.
This starts with the epididymis, but the epididymis stores sperm rather than making them. Only the seminiferous tubules produce sperm, so they must be first.
Correct. Sperm are made, stored, carried up, joined with seminal fluid, and released through the urethra.
This puts the ejaculatory duct before the ductus deferens, but the ejaculatory duct is formed from the end of the ductus deferens. It must come after the long ductus, just before the urethra.
questions.answerText: Seminiferous tubules, epididymis, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra

questions.q: Which list names the three accessory glands of the male reproductive system?
options: Prostate, bulbourethral glands, greater vestibular glands
questions.why: The male accessory glands add fluid to sperm to form semen. The paired seminal vesicles sit behind the bladder, the single prostate surrounds the first part of the urethra, and the paired bulbourethral glands lie just below the prostate. None of them make sperm; they make the fluid that carries and protects it.
notes: The epididymis is a duct where sperm are stored and gain motility, not a gland that adds fluid. Pick it if the question asked which part of the duct system sits on the testis.
Correct. These three glands add fluid to the sperm to form semen.
The greater vestibular glands are female glands beside the vaginal opening that secrete mucus. Pick them if the question asked which female glands secrete lubricating mucus.
The testes are the gonads that make sperm, not accessory glands. Choose them if the question asked which organs produce sperm and testosterone.

questions.q: Which accessory gland adds an alkaline, fructose-rich fluid that makes up the largest share of semen?
questions.why: The seminal vesicles produce an alkaline fluid rich in fructose, a sugar the sperm use for energy, and this fluid makes up about 60 percent of semen. The prostate adds a milky fluid that helps sperm stay active. The bulbourethral glands add an alkaline mucus that neutralizes traces of urine in the urethra and lubricates it.
notes: Correct. The seminal vesicles add the alkaline, fructose-rich fluid that forms most of the semen.
The prostate adds a milky fluid that helps sperm stay active. Pick it if the question asked which gland surrounds the urethra and adds a milky fluid.
The epididymis is a duct that stores sperm, not an accessory gland. Pick it if the question asked where sperm gain the ability to move.

The bulbourethral glands add a small amount of alkaline mucus that neutralizes urine in the urethra and lubricates it. Choose them if the question asked which glands clear the urethra before ejaculation.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the columns of erectile tissue in the penis?
options: One dorsal corpus spongiosum and two ventral corpora cavernosa around the urethra
Two dorsal corpora spongiosa and one ventral corpus cavernosum around the urethra
Three corpora cavernosa side by side, with the urethra running between them
Two dorsal corpora cavernosa and one ventral corpus spongiosum around the urethra
questions.why: The penis has three columns of erectile tissue. The paired corpora cavernosa run along the dorsal side, and the single corpus spongiosum runs along the ventral side and surrounds the spongy urethra. The corpus spongiosum expands at the tip to form the glans penis.
notes: This flips the columns top to bottom. The single column is ventral, and it is the one that holds the urethra.
This gets the positions right but swaps the names. The urethra runs through the spongiosum, which is how the spongy urethra gets its name.
There are only two corpora cavernosa, and the urethra does not run between columns. It runs inside the single corpus spongiosum.
Correct. Two dorsal corpora cavernosa sit above one ventral corpus spongiosum, which holds the urethra.
questions.answerText: Two dorsal corpora cavernosa and one ventral corpus spongiosum around the urethra

questions.q: Why can an enlarged prostate make urination difficult?
options: The urethra runs through the prostate, which squeezes it as it grows
The prostate presses on both ureters, blocking urine from the kidneys
The prostate presses on the external urethral sphincter and paralyzes it
The prostate grows into the bladder and blocks the detrusor muscle
questions.why: The prostate is a gland that wraps around the first part of the male urethra just below the bladder, a segment called the prostatic urethra. When the prostate enlarges, as in benign prostatic hyperplasia (a non-cancerous overgrowth), it squeezes the urethra running through it. The urine stream weakens and the bladder may not empty fully, which is how a reproductive organ causes a urinary symptom.
notes: Correct. The urethra runs through the prostate, so prostate enlargement squeezes it.

The ureters enter the bladder at the back of the trigone, above the prostate, so an enlarged prostate does not usually squeeze them. Pick the ureters if the question asked which tubes carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.

The external urethral sphincter is a ring of skeletal muscle below the prostate that gives voluntary control. Prostate enlargement narrows the urethra itself rather than paralyzing this muscle; pick the external sphincter if the question asked which muscle gives conscious control over urination.
The prostate sits below the bladder and surrounds the urethra; the detrusor in the bladder wall is still able to contract. The problem is a narrowed outlet, not a blocked muscle.
questions.answerText: The urethra runs through the prostate, which squeezes it as it grows

questions.q: Which part of a sperm cell holds the centrioles?
questions.why: The neck is the short, narrow part just behind the head. It holds the centrioles, and the core of microtubules that runs the length of the tail starts here.
notes: The middle piece is packed with mitochondria that make ATP to power the tail. It comes just after the neck.
Correct. The neck, just behind the head, holds the centrioles.
The acrosome is the cap over the front of the head. It holds enzymes that help the sperm get through the layers around the oocyte.
The end piece is the short, thin tip at the very end of the tail, the opposite end from the centrioles.

questions.q: Which list gives the parts of the sperm tail in order, from the head to the tip?
options: Middle piece, neck, principal piece, end piece
Neck, middle piece, principal piece, end piece
Neck, principal piece, middle piece, end piece
Neck, middle piece, end piece, principal piece
questions.why: The tail is a long flagellum with four parts. The short neck sits just behind the head, then comes the middle piece packed with mitochondria, then the long principal piece, and finally the thin end piece at the tip.
notes: The neck comes first, right behind the head. The middle piece follows it.
Correct. From the head back, the tail runs neck, middle piece, principal piece, end piece.
The middle piece comes before the principal piece. The mitochondria sit in the first long stretch of the tail, right after the neck.
The end piece is the very tip, so it comes last. The principal piece, the longest part, comes before it.
questions.answerText: Neck, middle piece, principal piece, end piece

questions.q: A sperm cell has a normal head and a normal middle piece, but it cannot drive itself forward. Which part is most likely defective?
questions.why: The principal piece is the longest part of the tail and does most of the whipping that moves the cell forward. The middle piece makes the ATP that powers the tail, and here it is normal. So a sperm that cannot swim forward points to a problem in the principal piece.
notes: Correct. The principal piece does most of the whipping that moves the sperm forward.
The acrosome is the enzyme cap over the head. It helps the sperm get through the layers around the oocyte, not swim.
The nucleus fills most of the head and holds the 23 chromosomes. The head is normal here, and the nucleus does not move the cell.
The end piece is only the short, thin tip of the tail. The principal piece, the longest part, does most of the whipping.

questions.q: Which pairing of a sperm cell part with what it holds is correct?
questions.why: Each part of a sperm cell holds something specific. The head holds the nucleus, capped by the enzyme-filled acrosome. The neck holds the centrioles, the middle piece is packed with mitochondria, and the principal and end pieces make up the rest of the tail.
notes: The middle piece holds mitochondria that make ATP for the tail. The enzymes that digest a path to the oocyte are in the acrosome.
The end piece is the short, thin tip of the tail. The mitochondria wind in a spiral around the middle piece, the only part packed with them.
The 23 chromosomes are in the nucleus, which fills most of the head. The acrosome is the cap over the front of the nucleus and holds enzymes.
Correct. The neck, just behind the head, holds the centrioles, and the core of the tail starts there.

questions.q: On a sperm smear, which part is the dark, densely stained oval at the front, and what makes up most of it?
options: The middle piece, which is mostly mitochondria
The head, which is mostly the nucleus
The neck, which is mostly centrioles
The acrosome, which is mostly mitochondria
questions.why: On a sperm smear, the head stains as a dark, dense oval and the tail is the long thin line behind it. The head is a flattened oval made mostly of the nucleus, which holds 23 chromosomes, with almost no cytoplasm. The acrosome forms a cap over the front of that nucleus.
notes: The middle piece is packed with mitochondria, but it is part of the tail, behind the neck. The dark oval at the front is the head.
Correct. The head is the dark oval, and most of it is the nucleus with almost no cytoplasm.
The neck is the short, narrow part just behind the head that holds the centrioles. It is too small to be the dark oval at the front.
The acrosome is the cap over the front of the head, and it holds enzymes, not mitochondria. Most of the dark oval is the nucleus.
questions.answerText: The head, which is mostly the nucleus

questions.q: A sperm cell swims normally, but the cap over the front of its nucleus never formed. Which part is missing, and what would this sperm be unable to do?
options: The middle piece; it could not make ATP to swim
The nucleus; it could not deliver its 23 chromosomes
The acrosome; it could not get through to the oocyte
The neck; it could not start the core of the tail
questions.why: The acrosome is the cap that covers the front of the nucleus in the sperm head. It is a sac of enzymes that lets the sperm digest a path through the layers around the oocyte. Swimming depends on the tail and its mitochondria, so this sperm could reach the oocyte but could not get through to it.
notes: The middle piece holds the mitochondria that power the tail, and this sperm swims normally. The missing cap over the nucleus is the acrosome.
The nucleus is what the cap covers, and it is still present. Losing the cap removes the enzymes, not the chromosomes.
Correct. The missing cap is the acrosome, the sac of enzymes that lets a sperm digest its way through the layers around the oocyte.
The neck is behind the head and holds the centrioles where the tail core starts. It is not a cap over the nucleus, and the tail here works fine.
questions.answerText: The acrosome; it could not get through to the oocyte

questions.q: In a cross section of the penis, you find a small opening surrounded by a single column of erectile tissue, with two larger columns side by side above it. What is the opening, and which surface of the penis is at the top of this view?
options: The spongy urethra, with the ventral surface at the top
The spongy urethra, with the dorsal surface at the top
The prostatic urethra, with the dorsal surface at the top
The ejaculatory duct, with the ventral surface at the top
questions.why: Start a penis cross section by finding the urethra. The single column wrapped around it is the corpus spongiosum, which lies on the ventral side and surrounds the spongy urethra. The two larger columns side by side are the corpora cavernosa, which lie on the dorsal side, so the view has the dorsal surface at the top.
notes: The opening is right, but the corpus spongiosum around it is ventral. The two corpora cavernosa above it are dorsal, so the top of this view is dorsal.
Correct. The column around the urethra is the corpus spongiosum on the ventral side, so the two corpora cavernosa above it mark the dorsal side.
The prostatic urethra runs through the prostate just below the bladder, not through the penis. The urethra inside the corpus spongiosum is the spongy urethra.
The ejaculatory ducts form where the seminal vesicle ducts join the ductus deferens, inside the pelvis. The opening ringed by erectile tissue in the penis is the spongy urethra.
questions.answerText: The spongy urethra, with the dorsal surface at the top

questions.q: On a model, you trace the corpus spongiosum from the tip of the penis back to the perineum. What does it form at the tip, and what does it form in the root?
options: The crura at the tip and the glans in the root
The prepuce at the tip and the bulb of the penis in the root
The glans at the tip and the crura in the root
The glans at the tip and the bulb of the penis in the root
questions.why: The corpus spongiosum is the single ventral column of erectile tissue that surrounds the spongy urethra. At the tip it expands to form the glans penis. At its back end in the root it forms the bulb of the penis, while the crura of the root belong to the two corpora cavernosa.
notes: This puts the parts backward. The glans is the enlarged tip, and the crura are back in the root, where they belong to the corpora cavernosa.
The prepuce is the loose fold of skin over the glans, not erectile tissue. The corpus spongiosum itself expands into the glans.
The glans is right, but the crura are the back ends of the two corpora cavernosa, attached to the ischial and pubic rami. The corpus spongiosum ends in the bulb.
Correct. The corpus spongiosum expands to form the glans at the tip, and its back end is the bulb of the penis in the root.
questions.answerText: The glans at the tip and the bulb of the penis in the root

questions.q: In a varicocele, which network of veins swells and twists?
questions.why: The veins of the testis run up the spermatic cord as a network called the pampiniform plexus. In a varicocele these veins swell and twist, above the testis. Varicoceles are more common on the left, where the testicular vein drains into the left renal vein.
notes: Correct. A varicocele is swelling and twisting of the veins of the pampiniform plexus in the spermatic cord.
The seminiferous tubules are the sperm-forming tubules inside the testis, where testicular cancer usually begins. They are not veins.
The tunica vaginalis is the two-layered covering around the testis. Fluid collecting between its layers is a hydrocele, not a varicocele.
The inguinal canal is the passage in the abdominal wall that the testis descends through. A loop of intestine pushing into it is an inguinal hernia.

questions.q: In which part of the prostate does prostate cancer most often start?
options: The front part, farthest from the rectum
The tissue right around the urethra
The outer, posterior part, against the rectum
The upper part, where it touches the bladder
questions.why: The prostate sits just below the bladder and wraps around the prostatic urethra, with its back surface against the rectum. Prostate cancer most often starts in the outer, posterior part of the gland. Because that part lies against the rectum, a clinician can feel it through the rectal wall.
notes: Cancer most often starts in the posterior part of the gland. That is why a clinician can feel it through the rectal wall.
The tissue around the urethra is where benign prostatic hyperplasia most often happens. That growth squeezes the urethra, while cancer usually starts farther back.
Correct. Prostate cancer most often starts in the outer, posterior part, which lies against the rectum.
The prostate does sit just below the bladder, but cancer most often starts in the posterior part of the gland, against the rectum, not up where it meets the bladder.
questions.answerText: The outer, posterior part, against the rectum

questions.q: During development, where do the testes first form?
options: On the posterior abdominal wall, near the kidneys
Low in the pelvis, beside the urinary bladder
Inside the inguinal canal of the abdominal wall
In the scrotum, where they stay throughout life
questions.why: The testes form high on the posterior abdominal wall, near the kidneys. That starting point is why each testicular artery branches from the abdominal aorta. Later in development each testis moves down through the inguinal canal into the scrotum, and if it stops along the way the condition is cryptorchidism.
notes: Correct. The testes develop high on the posterior abdominal wall near the kidneys, then descend into the scrotum.
The testes form higher than the pelvis, near the kidneys, which is why their arteries branch from the abdominal aorta.
The inguinal canal is the passage the testis travels through on its way down. A testis found there has stopped partway, which is one form of cryptorchidism.
The scrotum is where the testes end up, not where they start. They must descend into it, which is why an undescended testis is possible.
questions.answerText: On the posterior abdominal wall, near the kidneys

questions.q: Which list contains only organs of the female reproductive system?
options: Ovaries, uterine tubes, uterus, urinary bladder
questions.why: The female reproductive system is built from the ovaries (the gonads), the genital tract that carries the oocyte and receives sperm (uterine tubes, uterus, and vagina), the external genitalia (the vulva), and the mammary glands. Every organ in the correct list belongs to that system. Each of the other lists slips in one neighbor from the pelvis or from the male system.
notes: Correct. All four are organs of the female reproductive tract, running from the gonad to the canal that opens to the outside.
The urinary bladder sits just anterior to the uterus, but it stores urine and belongs to the urinary system. It would fit a list of pelvic organs or urinary organs, not reproductive ones.
The ductus deferens is the male sperm duct that carries sperm from the epididymis toward the urethra. Pick it for a list of male reproductive ducts.
The rectum lies just posterior to the uterus and vagina, but it is the last part of the large intestine. It belongs on a list of digestive organs or pelvic organs.

questions.q: Which order correctly lists the layers of the ovary from the surface inward?
options: Germinal epithelium, tunica albuginea, cortex, medulla
Germinal epithelium, cortex, tunica albuginea, medulla
Germinal epithelium, tunica albuginea, medulla, cortex
Tunica albuginea, germinal epithelium, cortex, medulla
questions.why: The ovary is read from the outside in. Its surface is covered by the germinal epithelium, a single layer of low cuboidal cells. Just beneath it is the tunica albuginea, a whitish capsule of dense connective tissue. Deep to the capsule is the cortex, which holds the follicles, and at the center is the medulla, the looser connective tissue that carries blood vessels and nerves.
notes: Correct. Epithelium on the surface, capsule beneath it, follicles in the cortex, and vessels in the medulla.
This order places the cortex above the capsule. The tunica albuginea wraps the whole ovary just under the surface, so the follicle-filled cortex is always deep to it.
This order flips the two inner regions. The follicles sit in the cortex, which is outside the medulla, and the vessels run through the central medulla.

This order puts the capsule on the surface. The tunica albuginea lies just beneath the germinal epithelium, so the epithelium has to come first. Students who remember the testis capsule as the outer layer often make this swap.
questions.answerText: Germinal epithelium, tunica albuginea, cortex, medulla

questions.q: The ovary is the female gonad. Which male organ is its homolog, the structure that develops from the same embryonic tissue?
questions.why: Homologous structures develop from the same embryonic tissue in males and females, even though they look different in the adult. The ovaries and the testes are both gonads, the primary reproductive organs that make the gametes (oocytes or sperm) and secrete sex hormones. That shared role and origin is why they are counted as homologs.
notes: The prostate is a male accessory gland that surrounds the urethra below the bladder and adds fluid to semen. It would be the answer for a question about the gland that encircles the first part of the male urethra.
The scrotum is the skin pouch that holds the testes. Its female homolog is the labia majora, so pick the scrotum when the question starts from the labia majora.

The epididymis is the coiled duct on the back of the testis where sperm mature and are stored. It is part of the male duct system, so pick it if the question asked where sperm mature after leaving the testis.
Correct. The testis and the ovary are both gonads that produce gametes and hormones.

questions.q: Which order lists the regions of the uterine tube from the end near the ovary to the end at the uterus?
questions.why: The uterine tube begins at the infundibulum, the funnel-shaped end that opens into the pelvic cavity beside the ovary and is fringed by the fimbriae. Next comes the ampulla, the widest and longest part, where fertilization usually happens. The tube ends at the isthmus, the narrow, thick-walled segment that joins the uterus.
notes: Correct. Funnel near the ovary, wide middle where fertilization happens, then the narrow segment joining the uterus.
This order starts in the middle of the tube. The ampulla is the wide segment after the funnel, so the infundibulum has to come before it.
This order swaps the last two regions. The narrow isthmus is the segment that joins the uterus, so it comes last, after the wide ampulla.
This is the correct sequence run backward, from the uterus out to the ovary. It would be right if the question asked for the order from the uterus toward the ovary.

questions.q: The cervical canal runs through the cervix. At which opening does the canal open upward into the uterine cavity?
questions.why: The cervical canal is the passage through the cervix, the narrow lower part of the uterus. Its upper opening, the internal os, leads into the uterine cavity inside the body of the uterus. Its lower opening, the external os, leads into the vagina. Os means mouth or opening.
notes: The vaginal orifice is the opening of the vagina into the vestibule of the vulva, at the very bottom of the tract. It would be the answer for where the vagina opens to the outside.
The external os is the lower opening of the cervical canal, where it opens into the vagina. Pick it if the question asked where the canal opens into the vagina.

The vaginal fornix is the recess of the vagina that wraps around the outside of the cervix. It is a space in the vagina, not an opening of the cervical canal. Pick it if the question asked for the vaginal recess surrounding the cervix.
Correct. The internal os is the upper end of the cervical canal, opening into the uterine cavity.

questions.q: Which paired ligaments connect the uterus posteriorly to the sacrum?
questions.why: The uterosacral ligaments run from the cervix, the lower part of the uterus, back to the sacrum. They anchor the uterus from behind. Each uterine ligament is named for what it connects: the round ligaments reach the labia majora, the cardinal ligaments reach the lateral pelvic walls, and the broad ligaments are folds of peritoneum out to the lateral pelvic walls.
notes: The round ligaments are fibrous cords that run from the uterus forward and down to the labia majora. Pick them if the question asked which ligament reaches the labia majora.
The broad ligaments are folds of peritoneum that drape over the uterus and attach it to the lateral pelvic walls. They would be the answer for the peritoneal fold on each side of the uterus.
The cardinal ligaments run from the lateral pelvic wall to the cervix and vagina. Pick them if the question asked which ligaments anchor the cervix to the side walls of the pelvis.
Correct. The name says it: uterus to sacrum.

questions.q: Which pairing of a uterine wall layer with its tissue is correct?
questions.why: The uterine wall has three layers. The perimetrium on the outside is a serous membrane, part of the visceral peritoneum. The myometrium in the middle is the thick layer of smooth muscle, and myo means muscle. The endometrium on the inside is the mucous lining that sheds and rebuilds each cycle.
notes: The endometrium is the inner vascular mucosal lining, not a serous membrane. Pick the endometrium for a question about the lining that sheds in menstruation or where an embryo implants.
The perimetrium is the outer layer, and it is a serous membrane rather than muscle. Its correct pairing would be perimetrium and serous membrane.
The myometrium is muscle, not a serous membrane. This pairing mixes up the middle layer with the outer perimetrium, which is the serous layer.
Correct. The myometrium is the thick middle layer of smooth muscle.

questions.q: Which peritoneal pouch lies between the uterus and the rectum and forms the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in females?
questions.why: The peritoneum dips down between the pelvic organs to form pouches. Behind the uterus it drops between the uterus and the rectum to form the rectouterine pouch, also called the pouch of Douglas. This is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in females, so fluid, blood, or pus in the abdomen tends to collect there.
notes: Correct. The rectouterine pouch sits between the uterus and rectum and is the lowest point of the female peritoneal cavity.
The uterine cavity is the space inside the body of the uterus, where an embryo implants in the lining. It is inside the organ, not a peritoneal pouch outside it.
The vaginal fornix is a recess of the vagina that surrounds the cervix. It is inside the vagina, not a peritoneal pouch. It would be the answer for the vaginal recess around the cervix.

The vesicouterine pouch is the shallower peritoneal pouch in front of the uterus, between the uterus and the urinary bladder. Pick it if the question asked for the pouch between the bladder and uterus.

questions.q: What is the recess of the vagina that surrounds the cervix called?
questions.why: The cervix projects down into the top of the vagina. The vaginal wall wraps around it and forms a gutter-like recess all the way around the cervix, called the fornix. It is a space inside the upper vagina, which is why it is listed with the vagina and not with the uterus.
notes: The vestibule is the region between the labia minora that holds the vaginal and urethral openings. It is at the bottom of the vagina, not around the cervix. Pick it for the area of the vulva where the vagina opens.
The hymen is the thin fold of mucous membrane that partly closes the vaginal opening at the bottom of the vagina. It would be the answer for a question about the vaginal orifice, not the cervix.
Correct. The fornix is the vaginal recess that encircles the cervix.

The external os is the opening of the cervical canal into the vagina. It sits in the middle of the cervix, surrounded by the fornix. Pick it if the question asked where the cervical canal opens into the vagina.

questions.q: Which structure is part of the vulva, the external genitalia?
questions.why: The vulva is the collective name for the external genitalia. It includes the mons pubis, the labia majora and labia minora, the clitoris, the vestibule with the vaginal and urethral openings, and the greater vestibular glands. The labia minora are the two smaller, hairless skin folds that lie within the labia majora and enclose the vestibule.
notes: Correct. The labia minora are external skin folds and are part of the vulva.
The isthmus is the narrow segment of the uterine tube that joins the uterus. It is deep in the pelvis. Pick it for the part of the uterine tube closest to the uterus.
The fornix is the recess inside the upper vagina around the cervix. It is internal, so it is not part of the vulva. Pick it for a question about the vaginal recess that surrounds the cervix.
The cervix is the narrow lower part of the uterus that opens into the vagina. It is an internal organ region. Pick it for a question about where a Pap test samples cells.

questions.q: The greater vestibular glands secrete lubricating mucus beside the vaginal opening. Which male glands are their homologs?
questions.why: Homologs are male and female structures that develop from the same embryonic tissue. The greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands and the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands are both small, paired glands near the lower end of the tract that release mucus during arousal. Their matching position and mucus secretion reflect their shared origin.
notes: The seminal glands are paired male glands behind the bladder that add a large share of the fluid in semen. Pick them if the question asked which glands produce most of the seminal fluid.
Sebaceous glands are the oil glands of the skin that empty into hair follicles. They are found in both sexes, so they are not a male homolog. Pick them for a skin question about oil secretion.
Correct. The bulbourethral glands are the male homologs of the greater vestibular glands.
The prostate is a single male gland that surrounds the urethra just below the bladder. It would be the answer for the gland that encircles the first part of the male urethra.

questions.q: What is the diamond-shaped region between the thighs that holds the external genitalia and the anus called?
questions.why: The perineum is the diamond-shaped region bounded by the pubic symphysis in front, the ischial tuberosities on the sides, and the coccyx behind. It holds both the external genitalia and the anus, and it is divided into an anterior urogenital triangle and a posterior anal triangle.
notes: The vestibule is the small area between the labia minora that holds the vaginal and urethral openings. Pick it for the space where the vagina and urethra open.
The mons pubis is the cushion of fatty tissue over the pubic symphysis, at the top front of the vulva. Pick it for the fatty pad over the pubic bone.

The vulva is the collective name for the external genitalia only. It sits within the front part of the perineum but does not include the anus. Pick it for the collective term for the external female genitalia.
Correct. The perineum is the diamond-shaped region holding the external genitalia and the anus.

questions.q: Which ligaments support the breast by running through the mammary tissue to the skin?
questions.why: The suspensory ligaments (Cooper ligaments) are bands of connective tissue that run from the skin through the breast, between the lobes, to the fascia over the pectoralis major. They support the breast from within. A tumor that pulls on one of these ligaments can dimple the skin above it.
notes: The round ligaments belong to the uterus, not the breast. They are fibrous cords that run from the uterus through the inguinal canal to the labia majora.
The uterosacral ligaments belong to the uterus, not the breast. They run from the cervix back to the sacrum and anchor the uterus from behind.
The broad ligaments are in the pelvis, not the breast. They are folds of peritoneum that drape over the uterus and uterine tubes and attach them to the lateral pelvic walls.
Correct. The suspensory (Cooper) ligaments run through the breast to the skin and support it.

questions.q: Which description fits the broad ligament of the uterus?
options: A cord of tissue that anchors the ovary to the uterus
A band connecting the back of the uterus to the sacrum
A fold of peritoneum draped over the uterus and its tubes
A fibrous cord running from the uterus to the labia majora
questions.why: The broad ligament is not a cord but a wide double sheet of peritoneum. It drapes over the uterus, uterine tubes, and ovaries like a sheet over a clothesline and attaches them to the lateral pelvic walls. Blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and nerves run between its two layers to reach these organs.
notes: This describes the ovarian ligament, which ties the ovary to the side of the uterus. Pick this description when the question names the ovarian ligament.
This describes the uterosacral ligament, which connects the uterus to the sacrum. Pick this description when the question names the uterosacral ligament.
Correct. The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold draped over the uterus and tubes.
This describes the round ligament, which runs from the uterus to the labia majora. Pick this description when the question names the round ligament.
questions.answerText: A fold of peritoneum draped over the uterus and its tubes

questions.q: What kind of tissue makes up most of the clitoris?
questions.why: The clitoris is a small mass of erectile tissue at the front junction of the labia minora. Erectile tissue is a network of vascular spaces that fill with blood during arousal. This is the same kind of tissue found in the penis, and the clitoris is the female homolog of the penis.
notes: Glandular tissue secretes a product, and the clitoris is not a gland. Glandular tissue is the answer for the greater vestibular glands beside the vaginal orifice or for the mammary glands.
Lymphatic tissue is immune tissue that filters lymph, as in the lymph nodes, tonsils, and spleen. It does not form the clitoris.
Adipose tissue is fat, and it does not make up the clitoris. It is the answer if the question asked what the mons pubis is made of.
Correct. The clitoris is built of erectile tissue, like its male homolog.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares the internal os and the external os of the cervix?
options: Both open into the vagina, one on each side of the fornix.
Both open into the uterine cavity at opposite ends of the uterine body.
The internal os opens into the uterine cavity; the external os opens into the vagina.
The internal os opens into the vagina; the external os opens into the uterine cavity.
questions.why: The cervical canal is the passage through the cervix, and it has two openings. The internal os is the upper opening, on the inside, where the canal meets the uterine cavity. The external os is the lower opening, facing outward, where the canal meets the vagina. The words internal and external tell you which end is deeper in the body.
notes: Only the external os opens into the vagina. The fornix is the vaginal recess around the cervix, not a pair of openings, so this mixes up the fornix with the os.
The uterine cavity is reached only at the upper end of the canal. The lower opening leads into the vagina, so the two openings do not both open into the uterine cavity.
Correct. Internal os to the uterine cavity, external os to the vagina.
This reverses the two openings. The internal os is the deeper, upper end, so it opens into the uterine cavity, while the external os faces the vagina.
questions.answerText: The internal os opens into the uterine cavity; the external os opens into the vagina.

questions.q: Which structures are the female gonads, the primary reproductive organs?
questions.why: A gonad is the primary reproductive organ that makes the gametes and secretes sex hormones. In females the gonads are the ovaries, paired almond-shaped organs beside the uterus that produce oocytes and hormones. Every other female reproductive organ is an accessory organ that carries, receives, or supports.
notes: The uterine tubes catch the released oocyte and carry it toward the uterus. They transport the gamete but do not make it. Pick them for a question about where fertilization usually happens.
The uterus is the muscular organ where an embryo implants and a fetus develops. It supports a pregnancy but does not make gametes. Pick it for a question about where a fetus grows.
The mammary glands are modified sweat glands of the breast that produce milk. They are studied with this system but are not gonads. Pick them for a question about milk production.
Correct. The ovaries are the female gonads.

questions.q: What is the female gamete called?
questions.why: A gamete is a sex cell that carries half the genetic information and joins with a gamete from the other parent at fertilization. The female gamete is the oocyte, the egg cell. It develops inside an ovarian follicle and is released from the ovary at ovulation.
notes: The corpus luteum is the structure left in the ovary after the follicle releases its oocyte. Pick it for what remains after ovulation.
A follicle is the structure in the ovarian cortex that holds and supports a developing oocyte. It is the container, not the gamete itself. Pick it for the structure that houses an immature egg.
The zygote is the single cell formed when a sperm and an oocyte unite at fertilization. It is the product of two gametes, not a gamete. Pick it for the first cell of a new individual.
Correct. The oocyte is the female gamete, the egg cell.

questions.q: What is the collective term for the female external genitalia?
questions.why: The vulva, also called the pudendum, is the collective name for all the external female genitalia: the mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, vestibule, and greater vestibular glands. It is a group name, so it includes several smaller structures, each with its own name.
notes: The vagina is the internal fibromuscular canal from the cervix to the outside. It opens into the vulva but is not external genitalia. Pick it for the birth canal.
The perineum is the larger diamond-shaped region that holds the external genitalia and also the anus. Pick it for the whole region between the thighs, from the pubic symphysis to the coccyx.
The vestibule is one part of the vulva, the area between the labia minora that holds the vaginal and urethral openings. Pick it for that specific space, not the whole group.
Correct. The vulva is the collective term for the external genitalia.

questions.q: What is another name for the uterine tubes?
questions.why: The uterine tubes are also called the fallopian tubes, after the anatomist Fallopius, and some texts call them oviducts. They are the paired tubes that catch the oocyte at the ovary and carry it to the uterus. Eponyms like this are easy to mix up, so link fallopian with the uterus and ovary.
notes: The ductus deferens is a male duct that carries sperm from the epididymis toward the urethra. Because it is male, it cannot be another name for the female uterine tubes.
Correct. Uterine tubes and fallopian tubes are two names for the same paired tubes.
The lactiferous ducts are the milk ducts of the breast, one for each lobe, carrying milk to the nipple. They are not tubes of the pelvic reproductive tract.

The eustachian tubes are the auditory tubes that connect the middle ear to the pharynx, so they have nothing to do with the uterus. Students mix them up with the fallopian tubes because both names come from anatomists.

questions.q: What is the narrow inferior portion of the uterus that opens into the vagina called?
questions.why: The uterus has three regions from top to bottom: the dome-shaped fundus above the tube entries, the tapered central body, and the narrow cervix at the bottom. The cervix projects into the top of the vagina, and its canal opens into the vagina at the external os.
notes: The body is the tapered central portion of the uterus that surrounds the uterine cavity. Pick it for the main middle region, between the fundus and cervix.
The fornix is the recess of the vagina that wraps around the cervix. It is part of the vagina, not the uterus. Pick it for the vaginal recess around the cervix.
Correct. The cervix is the narrow inferior portion that opens into the vagina.
The fundus is the dome-shaped top of the uterus, above where the uterine tubes enter. It is at the opposite end from the vagina. Pick it for the superior portion of the uterus.

questions.q: What is the inner lining layer of the uterine wall called?
questions.why: The uterine wall has three layers, and the prefixes tell you where each one sits. Endo means within, so the endometrium is the inner lining that faces the uterine cavity. It is a vascular mucosa that thickens each cycle, sheds in menstruation, and is where an embryo implants.
notes: The myometrium is the thick middle layer of smooth muscle. Myo means muscle. Pick it for the layer that contracts during childbirth.
The tunica albuginea is the whitish connective tissue capsule beneath the surface of the ovary. It is not part of the uterus. Pick it for the capsule of the ovary.
The perimetrium is the outer serous layer of the uterus, part of the visceral peritoneum. Peri means around. Pick it for the outermost layer.
Correct. The endometrium is the inner lining of the uterus.

questions.q: Which structure is the fibromuscular canal that runs from the cervix to the body exterior?
