A primary follicle has cuboidal granulosa cells around the oocyte and a forming zona pellucida, but no fluid pockets and no theca yet. The fluid pockets here mean it has moved past that stage.
Correct. Several granulosa layers, a theca, and small fluid pockets mark a secondary follicle, and the next stage has one large antrum.
questions.answerText: A secondary follicle, which becomes a mature follicle

questions.q: An adult ovary slide shows a pale, white patch of fibrous scar tissue in the cortex with no oocyte. What is this patch, and which structure did it form from?
options: A corpus luteum, formed from a ruptured mature follicle
A corpus albicans, from a corpus luteum that broke down
A mature follicle, formed from a secondary follicle
The tunica albuginea, formed from the germinal epithelium
questions.why: After ovulation, the granulosa and theca cells left behind form the corpus luteum, a large glandular body. When the corpus luteum breaks down, it becomes the corpus albicans, which means white body. On a slide it is a pale scar of fibrous tissue in the cortex, with no oocyte.
notes: The corpus luteum does form from the follicle cells left after ovulation, but it is a large glandular body, not a pale fibrous scar. The scar comes after it breaks down.
Correct. The corpus albicans is the pale fibrous scar left when a corpus luteum breaks down.
A mature follicle is a large structure with an oocyte and a fluid-filled antrum. A patch with no oocyte and only scar tissue is past ovulation.
The tunica albuginea is the dense connective tissue capsule just under the germinal epithelium, covering the whole ovary. It is a layer, not a patch inside the cortex.
questions.answerText: A corpus albicans, from a corpus luteum that broke down

questions.q: On a model, you trace a uterine tube from the end that drapes over the ovary toward the uterus, and your finger stops on the widest, longest stretch. Which regions has your finger already passed, and which region comes next?
options: Past the fimbriae and isthmus, with the intramural part next
Past the infundibulum only, with the fimbriae next
Past the fimbriae and infundibulum, with the isthmus next
Past the isthmus, with the infundibulum next
questions.why: From the ovary toward the uterus, the tube runs fimbriae and infundibulum, then ampulla, then isthmus, then the short intramural part. The ampulla is the widest and longest part, so your finger is there. It has already passed the fringed funnel at the outer end, and the narrow, thick-walled isthmus is next.
notes: The isthmus comes after the ampulla, so it cannot already be behind your finger. The intramural part comes after the isthmus.
The fimbriae are the fringe on the edge of the infundibulum at the outer end, so you pass them first. They do not come after the ampulla.
Correct. The widest, longest stretch is the ampulla, which comes after the fimbriae and infundibulum and before the narrow isthmus.
This runs the tube backward. The isthmus is the narrow part next to the uterus, so you would reach it after the ampulla, not before it.
questions.answerText: Past the fimbriae and infundibulum, with the isthmus next

questions.q: In an older patient, the uterus has slid down into the vagina. Weakness of which ligaments most likely allowed this, and where do they run?
options: The broad ligaments, a peritoneal fold to the lateral pelvic walls
The cardinal ligaments, from the cervix to the lateral pelvic walls
The round ligaments, from the uterus through the inguinal canal
The cardinal ligaments, from the uterus through the inguinal canal
questions.why: Four paired ligaments help hold the uterus, along with the pelvic floor muscles. The cardinal (transverse cervical) ligaments run from the cervix and upper vagina to the lateral pelvic walls, and they are the main support that keeps the uterus from sliding down. When the uterus drops into the vagina, the support that has failed is mainly this one.
notes: The broad ligaments are a double fold of peritoneum from the sides of the uterus to the pelvic walls. They drape the uterus, tubes, and ovaries, but the main support against sliding down is the cardinal ligaments.
Correct. The cardinal ligaments run from the cervix and upper vagina to the lateral pelvic walls and are the main support that keeps the uterus from sliding down.
The round ligaments run from the uterus through the inguinal canal to the labia majora. They help keep the uterus tipped forward, but they are not the main support against sliding down.
The cardinal ligaments are the right support, but they run from the cervix and upper vagina to the lateral pelvic walls. The route through the inguinal canal belongs to the round ligaments.
questions.answerText: The cardinal ligaments, from the cervix to the lateral pelvic walls

questions.q: A biopsy needle passes through the uterine wall from the peritoneal cavity side into the uterine cavity. Which layer does it cross second, and what tissue is that layer?
options: The perimetrium, a serous layer of peritoneum
The endometrium, a mucous lining with two layers
The stratum basalis, a layer of smooth muscle
The myometrium, a thick layer of smooth muscle
questions.why: The uterine wall has three layers from the outside in: the perimetrium, the myometrium, and the endometrium. Coming from the peritoneal cavity, the needle meets the perimetrium first, because it is the outer serous layer and part of the visceral peritoneum. The second layer is the myometrium, the thick middle layer of smooth muscle.
notes: The perimetrium is the outer serous layer, part of the visceral peritoneum, so a needle coming from the peritoneal cavity crosses it first, not second.
The endometrium is the inner mucous lining next to the uterine cavity, with a functional and a basal layer. It is the last layer the needle crosses, the third, not the second.
The stratum basalis is the deep layer of the endometrium, next to the myometrium, and it is part of the lining, not muscle. It is crossed after the myometrium.
Correct. From the outside, the needle crosses the perimetrium first and the smooth muscle of the myometrium second.
questions.answerText: The myometrium, a thick layer of smooth muscle

questions.q: A non-cancerous tumor of smooth muscle is found in the rounded top of the uterus, above where the uterine tubes enter. Which layer and region of the uterus is it in?
questions.why: Uterine fibroids are non-cancerous tumors of the smooth muscle of the myometrium. The fundus is the rounded top of the uterus, above the points where the uterine tubes enter, and it is also where the myometrium is thickest. So a smooth muscle tumor at the top lies in the myometrium of the fundus.
notes: Correct. A smooth muscle tumor arises in the myometrium, and the rounded top above the tubes is the fundus.
The perimetrium is the outer serous layer, and the cervix is the narrow lower part that projects into the vagina. Neither matches a smooth muscle tumor at the top.
The myometrium is the right layer, but the cervix is the narrow bottom of the uterus. The rounded top above the tubes is the fundus.
The endometrium is the mucous lining, not muscle, and the body is the main central part below the fundus. Tissue from the endometrium growing outside the uterus is endometriosis.

questions.q: A pea-sized swelling forms on one side of the vaginal orifice, slightly toward the back, where a gland's duct has become blocked. Which gland is it, and where does its duct normally open?
options: The hymen, which partly covers the vaginal orifice
A greater vestibular gland, whose duct opens into the vestibule
A greater vestibular gland, whose duct opens at the cervix
A bulbourethral gland, whose duct opens into the spongy urethra
questions.why: The greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands are a pair of pea-sized glands, one on each side of the vaginal orifice and slightly toward the back. Their ducts open into the vestibule, the space between the labia minora, and their mucus lubricates it. A blocked duct would swell right at that spot.
notes: The hymen is a thin fold of mucous membrane at the vaginal orifice. It is not a gland and has no duct to block.
Correct. The greater vestibular glands sit on each side of the vaginal orifice, slightly toward the back, and their ducts open into the vestibule.
The gland is right, but its duct opens into the vestibule at the outside, not up at the cervix at the top of the vagina.
Bulbourethral glands are the male glands beside the membranous urethra. They are the male match for the greater vestibular glands, but they are not found in the female.
questions.answerText: A greater vestibular gland, whose duct opens into the vestibule

questions.q: On a vulva model, two thin, hairless folds enclose a space that holds two openings. If you follow these folds forward to where they meet, what do they form there, and over which structure?
options: The labia majora, over the vestibule
The mons pubis, over the pubic symphysis
The hymen, over the vaginal orifice
questions.why: The thin, hairless folds that enclose the vestibule are the labia minora. At the front they meet over the clitoris and form its prepuce. The clitoris is the small erectile organ at the front of the vulva, and only its glans shows on the surface.
notes: Correct. The folds are the labia minora, and where they meet in front they form the prepuce over the clitoris.
The labia majora are the outer folds of skin and fat, outside the labia minora, and they are hair-covered after puberty. They are separate folds, not what the labia minora form.
The mons pubis is a rounded pad of fat over the pubic symphysis, in front of the folds. It is not formed by the labia minora.
The hymen is a thin fold of mucous membrane at the vaginal orifice, at the back of the vestibule. The labia minora meet at the front, not over that opening.

questions.q: On a model, a probe placed in the opening at the back of the vestibule slides up a canal until it reaches a recess that rings a structure poking down into the top of the canal. What is the canal, and what is the recess?
options: The cervical canal, ending at the internal os
The urethra, ending at the neck of the bladder
The vagina, ending at the vestibule around the cervix
The vagina, ending at the fornix around the cervix
questions.why: The vestibule holds two openings, the external urethral orifice in front and the vaginal orifice behind it. A probe in the back opening runs up the vagina, which reaches from the vestibule to the cervix. The cervix pokes into the top of the vagina, and the recess that rings it is the fornix.
notes: The cervical canal runs through the cervix itself, from the external os to the internal os. The probe has to pass up the vagina before it reaches the cervix.
The urethral orifice is the front opening of the vestibule, not the back one. The urethra also has no recess ringing a structure at its top.
The canal is right, but the vestibule is the space between the labia minora at the outside. The recess around the cervix at the top of the vagina is the fornix.
Correct. The back opening of the vestibule is the vaginal orifice, and the recess ringing the cervix at the top of the vagina is the fornix.
questions.answerText: The vagina, ending at the fornix around the cervix

questions.q: Which sequence traces milk from where it is made to where it leaves the breast?
options: Alveoli, lactiferous sinus, lobule ducts, lactiferous duct, nipple
Lactiferous duct, alveoli, lobule ducts, lactiferous sinus, nipple
Alveoli, lobule ducts, lactiferous duct, lactiferous sinus, nipple
Areola, lactiferous sinus, lactiferous duct, alveoli, nipple
questions.why: Milk is secreted by the gland cells of the alveoli inside each lobule. Small ducts carry it out of the lobule into the one lactiferous duct that drains that lobe. Just before the nipple the duct widens into a lactiferous sinus where milk collects, and then it leaves through openings on the nipple.
notes: The lactiferous sinus is the widened end of the lactiferous duct, just before the nipple. It comes after the ducts, not before them.
The alveoli are where milk is made, so they come first. The lactiferous duct comes after the small lobule ducts.
Correct. Milk is made in the alveoli, drains through small ducts and a lactiferous duct, collects in the sinus, and leaves at the nipple.
This runs mostly backward and starts at the areola, which is the ring of pigmented skin around the nipple. Milk is made in the alveoli and moves outward to the nipple.
questions.answerText: Alveoli, lobule ducts, lactiferous duct, lactiferous sinus, nipple

questions.q: Both the small bumps on the areola and the small sacs deep in the lobules are glands. Which statement correctly compares them?
options: The bumps are alveoli that secrete milk; the sacs are sebaceous areolar glands.
Both are alveoli that secrete milk, one set on the skin and one set deep inside.
The bumps are lactiferous sinuses; the sacs are lobules that hold the lobes.
The bumps are sebaceous areolar glands; the sacs are alveoli that secrete milk.
questions.why: The areola is the ring of pigmented skin around the nipple, and its small bumps are areolar glands, a type of sebaceous gland. The milk-making units sit deep in the breast: each lobule holds clusters of alveoli, small sacs lined with cells that secrete milk. Both are glands, but only the alveoli are part of the milk pathway.
notes: This swaps the two. Alveoli sit deep inside the lobules and secrete milk, while the bumps on the areola are areolar glands, a type of sebaceous gland.
Alveoli are found only inside the lobules. The bumps on the areola are a different kind of gland, the sebaceous areolar glands.

A lactiferous sinus is the widened end of a lactiferous duct just inside the nipple, not a bump on the areola. Lobules are subdivisions of a lobe, not the other way around, and the sacs inside them are alveoli.
Correct. The areolar bumps are sebaceous glands, while the alveoli inside the lobules are the sacs that secrete milk.
questions.answerText: The bumps are sebaceous areolar glands; the sacs are alveoli that secrete milk.

questions.q: A breast tumor pulls on a band of connective tissue that runs from the skin to the fascia over the pectoralis major, and the skin over it dimples. Which structure is being pulled, and between which units of the gland does it run?
options: A lactiferous duct, running between the lobules
A suspensory ligament, running between the lobes
A suspensory ligament, running inside each alveolus
The areola, running between the nipple and the skin
questions.why: The suspensory (Cooper) ligaments are bands of connective tissue that run from the skin through the breast, between the lobes, to the fascia over the pectoralis major. They support the breast. Because they are attached to the skin, a tumor that pulls on one can dimple the skin above it.
notes: A lactiferous duct carries milk from one lobe to the nipple. It is a duct, not a band of connective tissue tied to the skin and fascia.
Correct. Suspensory ligaments run from the skin between the lobes to the pectoral fascia, so a tumor pulling on one dimples the skin.
The structure is right, but alveoli are tiny secretory sacs inside lobules. The suspensory ligaments run between the much larger lobes.
The areola is the ring of pigmented skin around the nipple. It is skin, not a band that runs through the breast to the fascia.
questions.answerText: A suspensory ligament, running between the lobes

questions.q: A lactiferous duct is blocked just before the nipple. How much of the gland can no longer drain milk out through the nipple, and why?
options: Only the areolar glands, because the duct drains the areola
The whole breast, because all lobes share one duct
One lobe, because each lobe drains by its own lactiferous duct
One lobule, because each lobule has its own lactiferous duct
questions.why: The mammary gland has 15 to 20 lobes, and each lobe drains by its own lactiferous duct to the nipple. Blocking one duct just before the nipple cuts off the drainage of that single lobe. The other lobes still drain through their own ducts.
notes: Areolar glands are sebaceous glands on the areola, not part of the milk pathway. The lactiferous duct carries milk from a lobe.
The lobes do not share a duct. Each of the 15 to 20 lobes has its own lactiferous duct, so the others keep draining.
Correct. There is one lactiferous duct per lobe, so blocking one duct stops drainage from that one lobe.
Lobules drain by small ducts that join into the lactiferous duct for the whole lobe. A lactiferous duct serves an entire lobe, not a single lobule.
questions.answerText: One lobe, because each lobe drains by its own lactiferous duct

questions.q: A mammary gland slide shows small sacs lined with secretory cells, each wrapped by contractile cells. What are the sacs, and what do the wrapping cells do?
options: Alveoli, wrapped by myoepithelial cells that push out milk
Lobes, wrapped by suspensory ligaments that support them
Alveoli, wrapped by sebaceous cells that oil the nipple
Lactiferous sinuses, wrapped by smooth muscle that stores milk
questions.why: Each lobule holds clusters of alveoli, small sacs lined with cells that secrete milk. Myoepithelial cells around the alveoli contract to push the milk out into the ducts. From there it moves through the lactiferous duct toward the nipple.
notes: Correct. The secretory sacs are alveoli, and the myoepithelial cells around them contract to push milk into the ducts.
Lobes are the 15 to 20 large compartments of the gland, far bigger than a sac on a slide. Suspensory ligaments run between lobes but are not contractile cells.
The sacs are alveoli, but the cells around them are myoepithelial cells that contract. Sebaceous glands on the breast are the areolar glands on the areola.
A lactiferous sinus is the widened end of a lactiferous duct near the nipple where milk collects. The secretory sacs that make milk are the alveoli.
questions.answerText: Alveoli, wrapped by myoepithelial cells that push out milk

questions.q: Which structure secretes gonadotropin releasing hormone?
questions.why: GnRH is made by a small population of hypothalamic neurons whose axons end at the median eminence. The anterior pituitary is the target of GnRH, not its source, and it responds by releasing LH and FSH. The posterior pituitary stores oxytocin and ADH made in the hypothalamus, but GnRH is not among them. The gonads sit at the bottom of the axis and send hormones back up, so they are the end of the chain rather than the start.

questions.q: By what route does gonadotropin releasing hormone reach the anterior pituitary?
options: By axonal transport down the infundibulum to the gland
By diffusion across the sella turcica
Through the hypothalamic hypophyseal portal veins
questions.why: The portal veins carry GnRH from the median eminence directly to the gonadotropes, so a tiny amount of hormone reaches a high local concentration. If GnRH had to travel through the general circulation it would be diluted and degraded long before arriving. Axonal transport down the infundibulum is how oxytocin and ADH reach the posterior pituitary, which is a different lobe with a different delivery system. Simple diffusion across bone is not a transport route the body uses.
questions.answerText: Through the hypothalamic hypophyseal portal veins

questions.q: Which two hormones does the anterior pituitary release in response to gonadotropin releasing hormone?
options: Luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone
Adrenocorticotropic hormone and thyroid stimulating hormone
questions.why: One releasing hormone drives both gonadotropins, which is why LH and FSH tend to move together when the hypothalamus changes its output. ACTH and TSH are also anterior pituitary hormones but they answer to CRH and TRH and run the adrenal and thyroid axes. Oxytocin comes from the posterior pituitary, and prolactin is anterior pituitary but is controlled mainly by dopamine inhibition rather than GnRH. Inhibin and activin are gonadal peptides that feed back on the pituitary rather than being released by it.
questions.answerText: Luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone

questions.q: In what pattern is gonadotropin releasing hormone normally released?
options: As a single large bolus once each morning
Only in the hours surrounding ovulation
In pulses, roughly every one to three hours
At a continuous steady level all day
questions.why: The gonadotrope requires a pulsatile signal, and the frequency of those pulses is itself information that shifts the LH to FSH ratio. A continuous steady level does the opposite of what students expect: it downregulates the GnRH receptor and shuts the axis off. A single daily bolus describes the pattern of some other rhythms, such as the cortisol morning peak, not GnRH. Release only around ovulation would leave the axis silent for most of the cycle, and the follicular phase depends on ongoing gonadotropin support.
questions.answerText: In pulses, roughly every one to three hours

questions.q: To which chemical class do luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone belong?
questions.why: LH and FSH are glycoprotein hormones built from a shared alpha subunit and a distinct beta subunit, so they act at surface receptors and cannot cross the plasma membrane. Steroids describe the gonadal hormones further down the axis, estrogen, progesterone and testosterone, which do enter cells and act on nuclear receptors. Catecholamines such as epinephrine are tyrosine derivatives from the adrenal medulla. Eicosanoids such as prostaglandins are made from arachidonic acid and act locally rather than as pituitary messengers.

questions.q: Which gonadal hormone selectively suppresses follicle stimulating hormone without much effect on luteinizing hormone?
questions.why: Inhibin is the peptide that lets the gonad report gamete production separately from steroid production, and it acts on the gonadotrope to turn FSH down specifically. Testosterone and progesterone are steroids that suppress both gonadotropins, largely by slowing GnRH pulses at the hypothalamus. Activin is the counterpart of inhibin and pushes FSH up rather than down. This selectivity is why a person with damaged gamete producing tissue can show a high FSH while LH stays close to normal.

questions.q: From which precursor molecule are the gonadal steroid hormones synthesized?
questions.why: Every steroid hormone, gonadal and adrenal alike, is built by modifying the cholesterol ring system, which is why the synthetic pathways for these hormones overlap so heavily. Tyrosine is the precursor for thyroid hormone and the catecholamines. Tryptophan gives rise to serotonin and then melatonin. Arachidonic acid is the starting point for prostaglandins and other eicosanoids, which matter in labor but are not steroids.

questions.q: In males, and during most of the female cycle, what type of feedback do the gonadal steroids exert on the hypothalamus and pituitary?
questions.why: The default arrangement is negative feedback, so rising testosterone or estrogen slows GnRH pulses and reduces LH and FSH, keeping the axis stable. Positive feedback is the exception, appearing only when estrogen from the dominant follicle stays high for a day or more just before ovulation. Feedforward describes anticipating a disturbance before it happens, which is not how the gonadal steroids act here. An axis with no feedback would have no way to hold hormone levels in range.

questions.q: A patient is given a gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist as a continuous infusion for several weeks. What happens to luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone?
options: Both remain at their baseline levels
questions.why: After a brief initial flare, continuous exposure downregulates and desensitizes the GnRH receptor on the gonadotrope, so LH and FSH fall and the gonads go quiet. Sustained elevation would be the answer if the receptor did not desensitize, but pulsatility is exactly what the gonadotrope requires. A split response with LH up and FSH down would need something acting selectively, such as inhibin. Unchanged levels would mean the receptor ignored a continuous agonist, which is not what happens.

questions.q: Both gonads are surgically removed from an adult. Predict what happens to luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone.
options: Both fall, because there is no target organ
Both stay the same, because the pituitary is intact
Both rise, because negative feedback is lost
questions.why: Gonadal steroids and inhibin are the brake on the axis, so removing the gonads releases that brake and gonadotropins climb to high levels. Falling gonadotropins would require damage above the gonad, not below it, since the pituitary does not need a target to secrete. Unchanged levels would mean the axis has no feedback, which contradicts the whole design. A split response would require something suppressing LH selectively, and nothing here does that.
questions.answerText: Both rise, because negative feedback is lost

questions.q: A tumor secretes large amounts of inhibin into the circulation. Which pituitary hormone falls the most?
questions.why: Inhibin acts on the gonadotrope to suppress FSH specifically, so FSH drops while LH is only modestly affected. LH answers mainly to GnRH pulse frequency and to steroid feedback, so it does not track inhibin closely. TSH and ACTH belong to separate axes with their own releasing hormones and their own feedback signals, and inhibin does not reach into them. This selective suppression is the reason FSH is the better clinical marker of gamete producing tissue.

questions.q: The pituitary stalk is severed, cutting the hypothalamic hypophyseal portal vessels. Predict the effect on luteinizing hormone and follicle stimulating hormone.
options: Both are unchanged, because the pituitary is autonomous
LH falls while FSH climbs sharply
Both fall, because GnRH can no longer reach the gonadotropes
Both rise, because inhibitory input is removed
questions.why: The portal vessels are the only practical delivery route for GnRH, so cutting them starves the gonadotropes of their releasing signal and both gonadotropins fall. Gonadotropins are driven by a releasing hormone rather than held down by an inhibiting one, so removing hypothalamic input lowers them. Prolactin is the hormone that rises after stalk section, because dopamine is the inhibiting signal it loses. The pituitary is not autonomous for LH and FSH, and nothing in this lesion selectively suppresses one gonadotropin.
questions.answerText: Both fall, because GnRH can no longer reach the gonadotropes

questions.q: Estradiol from a dominant follicle stays above its threshold concentration for about two days. Predict the effect on luteinizing hormone.
options: LH stays flat until progesterone rises
LH oscillates around its previous mean
LH rises steeply into a surge
LH falls further, deepening the suppression
questions.why: Sustained high estradiol flips the hypothalamic and pituitary response from negative to positive feedback, and the result is the LH surge that triggers ovulation about a day later. Continued suppression is what happens at low or briefly elevated estradiol, which is the pattern for most of the follicular phase. Progesterone rises after ovulation as a consequence of the surge, so waiting for it reverses the order of events. Simple oscillation would mean estradiol carried no information about follicle maturity.
questions.answerText: LH rises steeply into a surge

questions.q: A man takes exogenous testosterone. Predict what happens to his own luteinizing hormone secretion.
options: It falls, because testosterone feeds back negatively
It rises, to match the higher androgen level
It is unchanged, because the source is external
It rises first and then oscillates
questions.why: The hypothalamus and pituitary read total circulating androgen and cannot tell an injected molecule from one made by the Leydig cells, so LH is suppressed. Rising LH would require positive feedback from androgen, which does not exist in the male axis. The axis has no way to identify the source of a steroid, so calling it external does not exempt it from feedback. Sustained oscillation is not the pattern, because the suppression here is steady rather than intermittent.
questions.answerText: It falls, because testosterone feeds back negatively

questions.q: Laboratory results show low luteinizing hormone, low follicle stimulating hormone, and low gonadal steroids. Where does the problem lie?
questions.why: When the gonad fails, its steroids fall but the gonadotropins climb because negative feedback is lost, so low steroids with low gonadotropins points upstream to the hypothalamus or pituitary. Gonadal failure gives the opposite gonadotropin pattern and is the distinction worth memorizing. The adrenal cortex contributes androgens but is not the driver of LH and FSH. The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and ADH and has no role in the gonadal axis.

questions.q: A teenager has never entered puberty. Testing shows undetectable gonadotropin releasing hormone pulses, low luteinizing hormone, and low estradiol. Trace the axis and predict what happens if pulsatile gonadotropin releasing hormone is delivered by pump.
options: FSH rises but LH remains suppressed because it needs steroid priming
LH and FSH rise, then the ovary produces estradiol and follicles develop
LH and FSH stay low, because the pituitary has already atrophied permanently
Estradiol rises first and only later drives LH upward
questions.why: The lesion is at the top of the axis, so supplying the missing signal in its natural pulsatile pattern restarts everything below it: gonadotropes respond, gonadotropins rise, and the ovary makes estradiol and grows follicles. The pituitary in this situation is understimulated rather than destroyed, so it recovers once the signal arrives. Estradiol cannot come first, because the ovary needs gonadotropin support to make it. Both gonadotropins respond to GnRH, so a selective FSH only rise does not fit.
questions.answerText: LH and FSH rise, then the ovary produces estradiol and follicles develop

questions.q: The same gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist can be used either to start puberty or to shut the axis down. What determines which effect occurs?
options: Whether it is given before or after breakfast
Whether it is delivered in pulses or continuously
Whether the dose is high or low
Whether the patient is male or female
questions.why: The gonadotrope reads the pattern of the signal, not just its presence: pulsatile delivery keeps receptors responsive and stimulates the axis, while continuous delivery downregulates them and suppresses it. Dose matters at the margins but cannot convert continuous exposure into a stimulating signal. The pattern rule holds in both sexes, since the same receptor is on the same cell type. Timing relative to meals has no bearing on GnRH receptor regulation.
questions.answerText: Whether it is delivered in pulses or continuously

questions.q: A woman takes a combined oral contraceptive containing estrogen and progestin. Trace the axis and explain why she does not ovulate.
options: The pill blocks LH receptors on the follicle so the surge cannot act
The pill destroys the corpus luteum before ovulation can happen
The pill raises FSH so many follicles mature and none becomes dominant
Steady steroid levels suppress gonadotropins, so no LH surge forms
questions.why: Constant exogenous steroid holds the hypothalamus and pituitary under steady negative feedback, so gonadotropins stay low, no follicle reaches the estradiol output needed for positive feedback, and the LH surge never forms. Blocking LH receptors on the follicle is not how these steroids work, and it would not explain the low gonadotropins. The corpus luteum forms after ovulation, so it cannot be the thing preventing ovulation. FSH falls rather than rises, which is why multiple follicle recruitment is not the mechanism.
questions.answerText: Steady steroid levels suppress gonadotropins, so no LH surge forms

questions.q: A man using high dose anabolic androgens has a high serum testosterone but a very low sperm count. Which sequence explains the low sperm count?
options: Suppressed LH lowers intratesticular testosterone despite the high serum level
The androgen directly poisons the developing sperm cells in the tubule
High serum testosterone raises FSH and exhausts the Sertoli cells
The androgen disrupts the blood testis barrier so that sperm leak into the blood
questions.why: Spermatogenesis depends on a testosterone concentration inside the seminiferous tubule far above the level in blood, and that local concentration comes from Leydig cells driven by LH. Exogenous androgen suppresses LH, the Leydig cells go quiet, and intratesticular testosterone collapses despite a high serum value. Direct toxicity to germ cells is not the mechanism, and it would not explain why the effect reverses when the drug stops. FSH falls rather than rises under this feedback, and barrier leakage is not what these drugs do.
questions.answerText: Suppressed LH lowers intratesticular testosterone despite the high serum level

questions.q: Which testicular cell carries luteinizing hormone receptors and secretes testosterone?
questions.why: Leydig cells sit in the interstitial space between the tubules, respond to LH, and are the source of testosterone. Sertoli cells lie inside the tubule and carry FSH receptors instead, supporting the germ cells rather than making the main androgen. Spermatogonia are the dividing germ cells themselves and are the target of the hormonal support, not its source. Myoid cells are contractile cells around the tubule that help move sperm along and are not steroidogenic.

questions.q: Which testicular cell carries follicle stimulating hormone receptors and nurses the developing sperm?
questions.why: Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubule, bind FSH, and provide the physical support and nutrients that germ cells need as they mature. Leydig cells respond to LH and make testosterone from the interstitium outside the tubule. A spermatid is a stage of the germ cell being supported, so it is the recipient rather than the nurse. Epididymal cells handle sperm maturation and storage after the sperm have already left the tubule.

questions.q: Which hormone do Sertoli cells secrete to feed back on follicle stimulating hormone?
questions.why: Inhibin from the Sertoli cell is the feedback signal that tells the pituitary how well the tubule is working, and it selectively lowers FSH. Testosterone comes from the Leydig cell and suppresses both gonadotropins mainly by slowing GnRH pulses. Relaxin is a hormone of pregnancy, from the corpus luteum and placenta, with no role in this loop. Oxytocin is a posterior pituitary hormone acting on uterus and breast, not a Sertoli product.

questions.q: What is the function of androgen binding protein secreted by Sertoli cells?
options: It carries testosterone through the bloodstream to distant tissues
It blocks testosterone from reaching the germ cells
It keeps testosterone concentrated inside the seminiferous tubule
questions.why: Androgen binding protein holds testosterone in the tubular fluid at a concentration many times higher than in blood, which is the level germ cells require. Transport through the blood is handled by sex hormone binding globulin and albumin, which are different proteins with a different job. Conversion to dihydrotestosterone is done by the enzyme 5 alpha reductase, not by a binding protein. Blocking access would defeat the purpose, since germ cell development depends on high local androgen.
questions.answerText: It keeps testosterone concentrated inside the seminiferous tubule

questions.q: What forms the blood testis barrier?
options: The capillary endothelium of the testicular artery
Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells
A basement membrane around each spermatogonium
questions.why: Sertoli cells are joined to each other by tight junctions that split the tubule into a basal compartment and an adluminal compartment, isolating the developing sperm. Leydig cells sit in the interstitium and are not joined into a barrier. A basement membrane surrounds the whole tubule rather than each germ cell, and it does not create the compartment split. The capillary endothelium is leaky enough in the interstitium that it cannot be the barrier that hides sperm antigens.
questions.answerText: Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells

questions.q: Why does the immune system need to be kept away from developing sperm?
options: Sperm cannot survive contact with plasma proteins of any kind at all
Sperm appear after immune tolerance is set, so they read as foreign
Sperm carry bacterial antigens picked up from the epididymal duct
Sperm release histamine that would trigger inflammation
questions.why: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty, long after the immune system learned which antigens are self, so the haploid germ cells would be attacked as foreign without the barrier. Sperm do not acquire bacterial antigens in a healthy tract, so infection is not the explanation. Sperm are not a source of histamine, which comes from mast cells and basophils. Sperm do encounter proteins in seminal fluid and in the female tract, so blanket intolerance of plasma proteins is not the issue.
questions.answerText: Sperm appear after immune tolerance is set, so they read as foreign

questions.q: Which enzyme converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone?
questions.why: 5 alpha reductase makes dihydrotestosterone, the more potent androgen responsible for prostate growth and much of male external genital development. Aromatase does something different, converting androgens into estrogens, and it operates in fat, brain, and Sertoli cells. 17 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase works earlier in the pathway, making testosterone from androstenedione. Cholesterol desmolase performs the first committed step of all steroid synthesis and is not specific to androgens.

questions.q: About how long does one full cycle of spermatogenesis take in humans?
questions.why: A spermatogonium takes roughly 64 to 74 days to become a mature spermatozoon, which is why treatments affecting sperm production take more than two months to show up in a semen analysis. Seven days is far too short for meiosis plus the whole remodeling of spermiogenesis. Fourteen days is the length of the luteal phase in the female cycle, a value students often import here by mistake. Six months overshoots and would make the process slower than any measured value.

questions.q: Sertoli cell function is selectively impaired so that these cells no longer respond to follicle stimulating hormone. Predict what happens to circulating inhibin and follicle stimulating hormone.
questions.why: Inhibin is a Sertoli product, so losing Sertoli responsiveness lowers inhibin, and with the brake off FSH climbs. A rise in inhibin with a fall in FSH describes the healthy tubule doing its job, the opposite of this lesion. Both falling would require damage to the pituitary as well as the tubule. Both rising is impossible here, because inhibin cannot rise from a cell that is not responding.

questions.q: A man has failure of the Leydig cells but intact pituitary function. Predict his luteinizing hormone and testosterone levels.
questions.why: The Leydig cell is the source of testosterone, so testosterone falls, and the lost negative feedback lets LH climb. Low LH with low testosterone would point to a hypothalamic or pituitary problem rather than a gonadal one, which is the key distinction. High LH with high testosterone would mean the feedback loop had stopped working at the pituitary end. Low LH with high testosterone is the pattern of exogenous androgen use, where the drug suppresses the axis.

questions.q: Human chorionic gonadotropin is given to an adult man. Predict the effect on his testosterone.
options: Testosterone rises, because hCG acts on the LH receptor
Testosterone falls, because hCG suppresses the pituitary
Testosterone is unchanged, because hCG acts only on ovarian tissue
Testosterone falls, because hCG competes with LH at the receptor
questions.why: Human chorionic gonadotropin binds the same receptor as LH and has a longer half life, so it drives Leydig cells to make more testosterone. It does not act as a pituitary suppressant, and the resulting testosterone rise is what eventually lowers LH. The LH receptor is present on Leydig cells as well as on ovarian cells, so the effect is not sex specific. hCG is an agonist rather than a competitive blocker, so it activates the receptor rather than silencing it.
questions.answerText: Testosterone rises, because hCG acts on the LH receptor

questions.q: A man is treated with a 5 alpha reductase inhibitor. Which effect is expected?
questions.why: Prostate growth depends on dihydrotestosterone rather than on testosterone itself, so blocking the converting enzyme shrinks that stimulus. Serum testosterone does not fall and may rise slightly, because the block is downstream of testosterone synthesis. LH is governed by testosterone and estradiol feedback, which the inhibitor leaves largely intact. Inhibin comes from Sertoli cells responding to FSH, a pathway this drug does not touch.

questions.q: An aromatase inhibitor is given to a man. Predict the effect on luteinizing hormone.
options: LH falls, because aromatase is required for GnRH release
LH rises, because estradiol contributes to negative feedback
LH falls, because testosterone accumulates and suppresses the axis
LH is unchanged, because only estrogen feedback matters in women
questions.why: A surprising amount of male negative feedback at the hypothalamus is carried by estradiol made locally from testosterone, so blocking aromatase removes part of the brake and LH rises. Testosterone does accumulate, but the net effect on the axis is disinhibition rather than suppression, since the estradiol arm is gone. Estrogen feedback is not exclusive to women, and this experiment is the classic demonstration. Aromatase is not part of the machinery that releases GnRH.
questions.answerText: LH rises, because estradiol contributes to negative feedback

questions.q: Trauma disrupts the blood testis barrier. What is the expected consequence?
options: Follicle stimulating hormone secretion is permanently abolished
An immune response is mounted against the man's own sperm
Testosterone synthesis by Leydig cells stops immediately
Sperm mature faster because nutrients reach them more directly
questions.why: The barrier hides haploid germ cell antigens from lymphocytes, so breaching it can expose those antigens and produce antisperm antibodies. Leydig cells sit outside the barrier in the interstitium, so their testosterone output does not depend on it. Faster maturation is not what happens, because the barrier also maintains the specialized fluid the germ cells need. FSH secretion is controlled by the pituitary and inhibin feedback and would not be permanently abolished by local trauma.
questions.answerText: An immune response is mounted against the man's own sperm

questions.q: Why is testosterone from Leydig cells more effective at supporting spermatogenesis than an equal amount injected into a vein?
options: Leydig cell testosterone is chemically different from the injected form
Injected testosterone is destroyed before it leaves the circulation
Only Leydig cell testosterone can bind the androgen receptor
Leydig cells create a very high concentration right next to the tubule
questions.why: Spermatogenesis needs an intratesticular androgen concentration many times higher than blood, and only local production plus androgen binding protein can achieve it. The molecule itself is identical whether made or injected, so chemistry is not the difference. Injected testosterone is not destroyed in the circulation, and in fact raises serum levels well. The androgen receptor does not distinguish source, so receptor selectivity is not the explanation.
questions.answerText: Leydig cells create a very high concentration right next to the tubule

questions.q: A man has a normal testosterone, a normal luteinizing hormone, a high follicle stimulating hormone, and a very low sperm count. Which compartment is failing?
options: The Sertoli cells and seminiferous tubules
questions.why: Normal testosterone with normal LH says the Leydig compartment and its feedback loop are intact, while a high FSH with low sperm points to loss of inhibin from failing Sertoli cells and tubules. Leydig failure would show low testosterone and high LH instead. Pituitary failure would lower both gonadotropins rather than raise FSH. A hypothalamic lesion would also lower gonadotropins, so a high FSH argues against it. This is the pattern that shows why inhibin is worth learning as a separate signal.
questions.answerText: The Sertoli cells and seminiferous tubules

questions.q: A man whose pituitary gonadotropes were destroyed is given testosterone replacement. Predict his libido and his sperm count.
options: Libido stays low but the sperm count recovers
Both stay low because testosterone cannot act without LH
Libido is restored but the sperm count stays very low
Both libido and sperm count are restored to normal
questions.why: Systemic testosterone is enough for libido, muscle, and secondary sexual characteristics, but it cannot recreate the intratesticular concentration that only LH driven Leydig cells produce, and it does nothing for the missing FSH signal to Sertoli cells. Full restoration would require replacing the gonadotropins themselves, which is why fertility treatment in this situation uses hCG and FSH rather than testosterone. Recovery of sperm without libido reverses which effect systemic testosterone can deliver. Testosterone acts perfectly well at its receptors without LH, so total failure is not the outcome.
questions.answerText: Libido is restored but the sperm count stays very low

questions.q: A testis remains in the abdomen instead of descending into the scrotum. Predict the effect on spermatogenesis and on testosterone production.
options: Spermatogenesis is preserved while testosterone production fails
Both are unaffected, because the testis is perfused well in either location
Spermatogenesis is impaired while testosterone production is preserved
Both spermatogenesis and testosterone production stop completely
questions.why: The germ cell compartment is temperature sensitive and is damaged at core body temperature, while Leydig cells tolerate the higher temperature and continue making testosterone. Complete failure of both would predict a boy who never virilizes, which is not what is seen. The reverse pattern misassigns the temperature sensitivity, since it is the tubule rather than the interstitium that suffers. Perfusion is not the limiting factor here, temperature is, which is the whole reason the scrotum sits outside the body.
questions.answerText: Spermatogenesis is impaired while testosterone production is preserved

questions.q: Follow the chain from a gonadotropin releasing hormone pulse to a mature sperm. Which step would fail first if Sertoli cells could not make androgen binding protein?
options: Testosterone would not stay concentrated in the tubule, so maturation falters
Leydig cells would stop responding to LH, so testosterone synthesis would stop
The pituitary would stop releasing FSH, so Sertoli cells would lose their signal
GnRH pulses would slow, so the whole axis would shut down
questions.why: Androgen binding protein sits at the last link in the chain, holding testosterone in the tubular fluid where germ cells need it, so losing it breaks maturation while everything upstream still works. Leydig cells respond to LH regardless of what Sertoli cells secrete, so their synthesis continues. FSH release depends on GnRH and inhibin, not on androgen binding protein. GnRH pulse frequency is set by steroid feedback and would not change from the loss of a local carrier protein.
questions.answerText: Testosterone would not stay concentrated in the tubule, so maturation falters

questions.q: Which phase of the ovarian cycle begins on day 1?
questions.why: Day 1 is the first day of menstrual bleeding, and in the ovary that is the start of the follicular phase, when a cohort of follicles begins to grow under FSH. The luteal phase comes last, after ovulation, when the corpus luteum has formed. Ovulation is the brief event that separates the two, near the middle of the cycle rather than at its start. The secretory phase is a uterine phase name, and it lines up with the luteal phase of the ovary, not with day 1.

questions.q: Which ovarian phase has a nearly fixed length of about 14 days?
questions.why: The corpus luteum has a built in lifespan of roughly 14 days unless it is rescued, so the luteal phase is the constant one. The follicular phase is the variable part, which is why a 35 day cycle and a 21 day cycle differ mainly in how long it takes a dominant follicle to mature. Ovulation is a single event lasting hours rather than a two week phase. The menstrual phase is a uterine phase of about five days, not an ovarian phase of fourteen.

questions.q: Which hormone dominates the luteal phase of the ovarian cycle?
questions.why: The corpus luteum is primarily a progesterone factory, and progesterone is the signature hormone of the luteal phase. Estrogen dominates the follicular phase and rises again modestly in the luteal phase, but it is not the phase defining hormone. FSH is highest in the early follicular phase and is actively suppressed during the luteal phase. LH spikes at the surge and then falls back, so it is not the sustained luteal hormone.

questions.q: What does the ruptured follicle become after ovulation?
questions.why: The remaining granulosa and theca cells luteinize and become the corpus luteum, an endocrine structure that secretes progesterone and estrogen. The corpus albicans is the scar tissue that the corpus luteum leaves behind about two weeks later, so it is the next step rather than this one. A primordial follicle is the resting starting point of a follicle, not an end product. The zona pellucida is the glycoprotein coat around the oocyte and leaves with the egg.

questions.q: How long after the luteinizing hormone surge does ovulation typically occur?
questions.why: Ovulation follows the surge by roughly a day, which is why detecting the LH rise in urine gives useful advance notice. A few hours is too fast for the follicular wall to weaken and the oocyte to complete meiosis I. Five to seven days would put ovulation in the middle of the luteal phase, after progesterone has already risen. Fourteen days is the length of the whole luteal phase, a number students often attach to the wrong interval.

questions.q: Which follicular cells produce the androgens that granulosa cells then convert to estrogen?
questions.why: Theca cells respond to LH by making androgens, which cross to the granulosa cells where FSH driven aromatase converts them to estradiol. Granulosa cells are the converting half of that partnership and are not the androgen source. Luteal cells exist only after ovulation, so they cannot be supplying the follicular phase. Medullary stromal cells make small amounts of steroid but are not the two cell two gonadotropin partnership the follicle depends on.

questions.q: Which hormone from the growing dominant follicle helps suppress follicle stimulating hormone so the other follicles regress?
questions.why: Inhibin from granulosa cells, together with rising estradiol, pulls FSH down, and the dominant follicle survives the drop because it has the most FSH receptors. Relaxin belongs to the luteal phase and pregnancy, loosening connective tissue rather than tuning FSH. Progesterone stays low in the follicular phase and cannot be the signal that selects the dominant follicle. Oxytocin acts on uterus and breast and has no role in follicle selection.

questions.q: If fertilization does not occur, what happens to the corpus luteum?
options: It degenerates into the corpus albicans in about 14 days
It persists and continues to secrete progesterone indefinitely
It converts back into a primary follicle
It is shed along with the endometrium
questions.why: Without hCG to rescue it, the corpus luteum has a fixed lifespan and involutes into a fibrous corpus albicans, and its falling progesterone brings on menstruation. Persistence is what happens only when a pregnancy provides hCG. A corpus luteum cannot revert to a follicle, since the follicle cell population has already been irreversibly luteinized. The corpus luteum lies in the ovary, so it is not shed with the uterine lining.
questions.answerText: It degenerates into the corpus albicans in about 14 days

questions.q: A woman has a consistent 35 day cycle. Which phase is longer than in a 28 day cycle?
questions.why: The luteal phase is fixed near 14 days by the corpus luteum's lifespan, so all the extra time in a long cycle sits in the follicular phase while a dominant follicle takes longer to mature. Extending the luteal phase would require rescuing the corpus luteum, which happens only in pregnancy. Proportional stretching of both phases contradicts the fixed luteal length that makes cycle length prediction possible. Ovulation is an event of hours and does not stretch to fill extra days.

questions.q: A woman has a regular 35 day cycle. On approximately which day does she ovulate?
questions.why: Counting back the fixed 14 day luteal phase from day 35 puts ovulation near day 21. Day 14 assumes a 28 day cycle and is the most common error, since it counts forward from day 1 rather than backward from the next menses. Day 17 would be the midpoint of the cycle, but ovulation is not anchored to the midpoint. Day 28 would leave only seven days for the corpus luteum, which is shorter than its natural lifespan.

questions.q: During the early follicular phase, estradiol is low and rising slowly. What effect does it have on luteinizing hormone?
options: It raises LH slowly in proportion to its own rise
It suppresses LH through negative feedback
It drives an LH surge through positive feedback
It has no effect until progesterone appears
questions.why: At low concentrations and over short exposures, estradiol exerts classic negative feedback and keeps LH modest, which is the state for most of the follicular phase. Positive feedback appears only when estradiol is both high and sustained for a day or two, which is a late follicular condition. Progesterone is not required for estradiol to have an effect, and it stays low before ovulation. A smooth proportional rise would eliminate the sharp surge that ovulation depends on.
questions.answerText: It suppresses LH through negative feedback

questions.q: Progesterone rises after ovulation. What does it do to gonadotropin releasing hormone pulse frequency?
options: It leaves the frequency unchanged but raises pulse height
questions.why: Progesterone slows the hypothalamic pulse generator, which lowers LH and favors FSH on a per pulse basis while total gonadotropin output stays down. Speeding the pulses is the late follicular pattern that helps build toward the surge, not the luteal pattern. Pulses do not stop completely, since some gonadotropin support is needed to maintain the corpus luteum. Raising pulse amplitude without changing frequency is not the described effect of luteal progesterone.

questions.q: The luteinizing hormone surge acts on the dominant follicle. Which change does it produce in the oocyte?
options: The oocyte completes meiosis I and arrests in metaphase II
The oocyte completes meiosis II and becomes haploid
The oocyte begins meiosis I for the first time
The oocyte re-enters mitosis to produce more oocytes
questions.why: The oocyte has been arrested in prophase I since before birth, and the LH surge is the signal that lets it finish meiosis I and stop again at metaphase II. Meiosis II is completed only if a sperm fertilizes the egg, so it happens after ovulation rather than before. Meiosis I actually begins in fetal life, so the surge resumes it rather than starting it. Oocytes do not divide by mitosis after the fetal period, so no new oocytes are made.
questions.answerText: The oocyte completes meiosis I and arrests in metaphase II

questions.q: A woman has a regular 21 day cycle. Approximately how long is her luteal phase?
options: About 7 days, half of the shortened cycle
About 21 days, matching her cycle length
About 14 days, so she ovulates near day 7
About 10 days, scaled down with the shorter cycle
questions.why: The luteal phase holds near 14 days regardless of cycle length, so a 21 day cycle means the follicular phase is compressed to about a week and ovulation occurs around day 7. Scaling the luteal phase down assumes both halves stretch and shrink together, which is the misconception this card targets. A 7 day luteal phase would be a genuinely abnormal short luteal phase, not the expected finding. A luteal phase equal to the whole cycle would leave no time for follicle growth at all.
questions.answerText: About 14 days, so she ovulates near day 7

questions.q: Which observation best confirms that ovulation has already occurred?
options: A single high luteinizing hormone value
A fall in follicle stimulating hormone at midcycle
A rise in serum progesterone about a week later
A rise in serum estradiol in the days beforehand
questions.why: Progesterone only reaches high levels once a corpus luteum has formed, so a mid luteal progesterone rise is the retrospective proof that ovulation happened. Estradiol rises before ovulation and would be present even in a cycle where the surge failed. A high LH value shows a surge occurred but not that the follicle actually ruptured. A midcycle FSH fall accompanies dominant follicle selection and says nothing definitive about rupture.
questions.answerText: A rise in serum progesterone about a week later

questions.q: A gonadotropin releasing hormone antagonist is given on day 12 of a 28 day cycle. Predict the luteinizing hormone surge, ovulation, and the fate of the dominant follicle.
options: No surge, no ovulation, and the follicle persists without rupturing
The surge still occurs because estradiol acts directly on the ovary
Ovulation occurs early because the follicle is released from inhibition
The follicle luteinizes immediately and progesterone rises on schedule
questions.why: The surge is a pituitary event that requires GnRH signaling, so blocking the receptor prevents the LH rise, and without LH the follicle neither ruptures nor luteinizes. Estradiol drives the surge by acting on the hypothalamus and pituitary, not by acting on the ovary directly, so it cannot bypass the block. Nothing about this drug releases the follicle from inhibition, so early ovulation is backwards. Luteinization also depends on LH, so progesterone cannot rise on schedule. This is exactly why these antagonists are used to prevent premature surges in assisted reproduction.
questions.answerText: No surge, no ovulation, and the follicle persists without rupturing

questions.q: The corpus luteum is removed on day 20 of a nonpregnant 28 day cycle. Predict progesterone and the timing of menstruation.
options: Progesterone falls but menstruation is delayed past day 28
Progesterone is maintained by the ovary's other follicles
Progesterone falls and the next follicular phase is blocked
Progesterone falls sharply and menstruation begins early
questions.why: The corpus luteum is the sole significant source of progesterone in a nonpregnant cycle, so removing it drops progesterone at once, and endometrial support collapses, bringing menstruation forward. Delay would require continued progesterone, which is precisely what has been removed. Other follicles are not luteinized and cannot substitute as a progesterone source. Losing progesterone actually releases the axis, so the next follicular phase starts sooner rather than being blocked.
questions.answerText: Progesterone falls sharply and menstruation begins early

questions.q: An ovarian tumor secretes a constant high level of estradiol month after month. Predict follicle stimulating hormone and follicle recruitment.
options: FSH surges monthly and produces repeated ovulations
FSH is suppressed and normal follicle recruitment fails
FSH is elevated and many follicles are recruited each month
FSH is normal because only inhibin controls it
questions.why: Constant high estradiol holds the axis under steady negative feedback, so FSH stays low and the cohort of follicles that needs an FSH rise never gets recruited. Elevated FSH would require loss of feedback rather than an excess of the feedback hormone. Inhibin is one FSH regulator but estradiol is another, so calling FSH indifferent to estradiol is wrong. Repeated ovulations would require repeated surges, and constant rather than rising estradiol does not generate the surge pattern.
questions.answerText: FSH is suppressed and normal follicle recruitment fails

questions.q: Basal body temperature is recorded daily and rises about half a degree partway through the cycle, then stays up. Explain what caused the rise and what it tells you.
options: Falling FSH lowered heat loss, so a follicle is still maturing
Progesterone from the corpus luteum raised the set point, so ovulation is past
The estradiol peak raised the set point, so ovulation should occur in a day or two
The LH surge itself raised the set point, so ovulation is happening now
questions.why: Progesterone is thermogenic and shifts the hypothalamic temperature set point upward, so a sustained rise means a corpus luteum has formed and ovulation is already behind you. Estradiol does not raise the set point and in fact tends to lower it slightly, so it cannot be the source of the shift. The LH surge precedes the temperature rise by a day or more and is not itself thermogenic. FSH has no direct effect on thermoregulation. This is why temperature charting confirms ovulation retrospectively rather than predicting it.
questions.answerText: Progesterone from the corpus luteum raised the set point, so ovulation is past

questions.q: Which uterine phase corresponds in time to the follicular phase of the ovary?
questions.why: While follicles grow and pour out estradiol, the endometrium rebuilds itself, so the proliferative phase and the follicular phase are the same interval seen from two organs. The secretory phase lines up with the luteal phase instead, after progesterone appears. The menstrual phase is the first few days of the follicular phase, not the whole of it. Luteal is an ovarian term, not a uterine one, so it cannot be the uterine partner of anything.

questions.q: Which uterine phase corresponds in time to the luteal phase of the ovary?
questions.why: Once the corpus luteum forms and progesterone rises, the endometrium switches from growing to secreting, so the secretory phase and the luteal phase occupy the same days. The proliferative phase belongs with the follicular phase and its estradiol. The menstrual phase happens after luteal progesterone withdraws, at the very start of the next cycle. Follicular is an ovarian term and cannot label a uterine phase.

questions.q: Which hormone drives the proliferative phase of the uterine cycle?
questions.why: Estradiol from growing follicles stimulates mitosis in the endometrial stroma and glands, rebuilding the lining that was just shed. Progesterone acts on an endometrium estrogen has already built and turns it secretory instead. LH acts on the ovary rather than on the endometrium, so it drives this phase only indirectly. Inhibin acts on the pituitary to lower FSH and has no direct uterine effect.

questions.q: Which hormone drives the secretory phase of the uterine cycle?
questions.why: Progesterone from the corpus luteum converts a thickened endometrium into one with coiled glands secreting glycogen rich fluid, ready to receive an embryo. Estrogen builds the lining first but does not by itself make it secretory. FSH acts on granulosa cells in the ovary and has no endometrial receptor role here. Human chorionic gonadotropin appears only if an embryo implants, well after the secretory phase has begun.

questions.q: Which layer of the endometrium is shed during menstruation?
questions.why: The functionalis is the superficial layer supplied by spiral arteries, and it is the layer built up and then lost each cycle. The basalis is retained and is the source of the cells that regenerate the functionalis afterward. The myometrium is the smooth muscle wall and stays in place, contracting to help expel the shed tissue. The perimetrium is the outer serous covering and is never shed.

questions.q: What immediate hormonal change triggers menstruation?
options: A rise in both estrogen and progesterone
A rise in follicle stimulating hormone alone
A fall in luteinizing hormone alone
A fall in both estrogen and progesterone
questions.why: When the corpus luteum involutes, estrogen and progesterone both drop, the spiral arteries constrict, and the functionalis loses its blood supply and sloughs. A rise in these steroids maintains the lining rather than shedding it. FSH rises after menstruation begins as a consequence of the steroid withdrawal, so it follows rather than causes the event. LH has already fallen back after the surge, and its decline is not what times menstruation.
questions.answerText: A fall in both estrogen and progesterone

questions.q: In a standard 28 day cycle, which days make up the menstrual phase?
questions.why: Menstrual flow occupies roughly the first five days, and by convention the first day of bleeding is day 1 of the cycle. Days 6 to 14 describe the proliferative phase that follows. Days 15 to 28 describe the secretory phase after ovulation. Days 12 to 16 span the periovulatory window, which sits in the middle of the cycle rather than at the beginning.

questions.q: What does progesterone do to the endometrial glands during the secretory phase?
options: Makes them absorb fluid from the uterine cavity
Makes them coil and secrete glycogen rich fluid
Makes them divide rapidly and thicken the lining
Makes them constrict their spiral arteries
questions.why: Progesterone finishes the job estrogen started, turning straight glands into tortuous ones that secrete nutrient rich fluid to support an embryo before the placenta exists. Rapid division and thickening is the estrogen driven proliferative change that comes first. Spiral artery constriction happens when progesterone is withdrawn, not while it is present. The secretory endometrium adds fluid to the cavity rather than absorbing it.
questions.answerText: Makes them coil and secrete glycogen rich fluid

questions.q: A progesterone receptor blocker is given during the mid secretory phase. Predict the effect on the endometrium.
options: The lining continues to thicken through proliferation
The lining becomes more secretory than usual
The lining is unaffected because progesterone acts only on the ovary
The lining loses its support and begins to break down
questions.why: Progesterone is what holds the secretory endometrium together, so blocking its receptor mimics progesterone withdrawal and the lining sheds. Continued proliferation would need unopposed estrogen action, and the endometrium in this phase is already past that stage. Increased secretion would require more progesterone signaling, not less. Progesterone acts strongly on the endometrium, so calling its effect ovary only misplaces the target tissue.
questions.answerText: The lining loses its support and begins to break down

questions.q: A woman receives estrogen for many months with no progesterone. Predict the state of her endometrium.
options: It thickens continuously without becoming secretory
It becomes fully secretory and then sheds on schedule
It stays exactly at its baseline thickness
questions.why: Unopposed estrogen drives proliferation with nothing to stop it or convert it, so the lining keeps thickening and never organizes into a secretory pattern. Thinning is what a progestin alone would eventually produce, which is the opposite exposure. A secretory change requires progesterone, which by definition is absent here. Baseline thickness would mean estrogen had no proliferative effect, contradicting its central role in the proliferative phase.
questions.answerText: It thickens continuously without becoming secretory

questions.q: A woman has cycles in which no follicle ever ovulates. Which uterine phase never occurs?
questions.why: No ovulation means no corpus luteum, no progesterone, and therefore no secretory transformation, even though estrogen from developing follicles still drives proliferation. The proliferative phase does occur, because follicles produce estradiol whether or not they rupture. Bleeding still occurs, though it tends to be irregular breakthrough bleeding from an overgrown lining rather than true progesterone withdrawal menses. Saying all three occur ignores that the secretory phase has a strict hormonal prerequisite.

questions.q: What effect does luteal phase progesterone have on the myometrium?
options: It has no effect on smooth muscle
questions.why: Progesterone keeps the uterine muscle quiet, which protects a possible implantation and later maintains pregnancy. Increased contractility is the estrogen leaning state seen at term when the progesterone to estrogen balance shifts. Progesterone acts strongly on smooth muscle throughout the body, so no effect is wrong. Raising oxytocin receptor density is an estrogen effect near term, and progesterone tends to hold that number down.

questions.q: Cervical mucus is thin, watery, and stretchy at midcycle. Which hormonal state produces this?
questions.why: Peak estradiol just before ovulation thins cervical mucus so sperm can pass through it, which is the point of the change. High progesterone does the opposite, making mucus thick and hostile, which is a phase later and also part of how progestin contraceptives work. Both hormones high describes the mid luteal phase, where the progesterone effect dominates. Both low describes the menstrual phase, where mucus is scant rather than stretchy.

questions.q: What causes the ischemia that precedes shedding of the endometrium?
options: Loss of the stratum basalis blood supply
questions.why: Withdrawal of estrogen and progesterone triggers local prostaglandin release and spiral artery constriction, and the functionalis dies from the loss of perfusion. Dilation would increase blood flow and preserve the tissue rather than destroy it. Venous thrombosis is not part of the normal cycle. The basalis keeps its own straight arterial supply, which is exactly why it survives to regenerate the lining.

questions.q: An endometrial thickness measured on day 12 is much greater than one measured on day 3 of the same cycle. What explains the difference?
options: Falling FSH has allowed the lining to rebuild
Estrogen from growing follicles has driven proliferation
Progesterone from the corpus luteum has driven secretion
The LH surge has thickened the lining directly
questions.why: Day 3 is just after shedding, when only the basalis remains, and by day 12 estradiol has rebuilt a thick functionalis. Progesterone cannot be the explanation, because no corpus luteum exists before ovulation. The LH surge has not yet happened on day 12, and in any case it acts on the follicle rather than on the endometrium. FSH acts on granulosa cells, so its fall does not directly rebuild the lining.
questions.answerText: Estrogen from growing follicles has driven proliferation

questions.q: An endometrial sample taken on day 22 shows tortuous glands full of glycogen rich secretion. What does that tell you about the ovary?
options: An LH surge is about to occur within the next day
A functioning corpus luteum is present and secreting progesterone
A dominant follicle is still growing and secreting estradiol
The ovary has failed and produces neither steroid
questions.why: A secretory endometrium is direct evidence of progesterone action, and in a nonpregnant cycle the only meaningful progesterone source is a corpus luteum, so ovulation must have occurred. A growing follicle produces estradiol, which gives a proliferative rather than secretory picture. Ovarian failure would leave a thin inactive lining. An imminent surge belongs to the late follicular phase, when the endometrium is still proliferative.
questions.answerText: A functioning corpus luteum is present and secreting progesterone

questions.q: A woman's progesterone remains elevated past the expected day of menstruation and she does not bleed. What is the most likely sequence of events?
options: The corpus luteum involuted early and the endometrium became atrophic
Estrogen rose sharply and converted the secretory endometrium back to proliferative
FSH rose and recruited a new follicle that secreted the progesterone
An embryo implanted and hCG rescued the corpus luteum, so progesterone continued
questions.why: Human chorionic gonadotropin from the implanting embryo binds the LH receptor on the corpus luteum, keeping it alive past its normal 14 day lifespan, so progesterone never withdraws and menstruation never starts. Early involution would drop progesterone and bring bleeding forward, the opposite of what is described. Estrogen cannot reverse a secretory endometrium back into a proliferative one. New follicles make estradiol rather than progesterone, so recruitment does not explain the sustained level.
questions.answerText: An embryo implanted and hCG rescued the corpus luteum, so progesterone continued

questions.q: A woman ovulates normally but her luteal progesterone rises only to about half the usual level. Predict the endometrium and the length of her luteal phase.
options: Incomplete secretory development and a shortened luteal phase
Full secretory development and a normal 14 day luteal phase
Continued proliferation and a lengthened luteal phase
An atrophic lining with no bleeding at all
questions.why: Secretory transformation is dose dependent, so weak progesterone gives an endometrium that is out of step with the calendar, and the underperforming corpus luteum also involutes sooner, shortening the phase. Full development at half the hormone would mean the endometrial response has no dose dependence. Continued proliferation would require the absence of progesterone rather than a reduced amount, and less progesterone shortens rather than lengthens the phase. An atrophic non bleeding lining is what long term progestin exposure produces, which is a different situation.
questions.answerText: Incomplete secretory development and a shortened luteal phase

questions.q: Follow the cycle in order: estradiol climbs from day 6 to day 13, an LH surge occurs, then progesterone rises from day 16 onward. Match the uterine phases to those events.
options: Proliferative for the whole cycle, since estrogen is present throughout
Menstrual through day 14, then proliferative from about day 15 to 28
Proliferative through day 14, then secretory from about day 15 to 28
Secretory through day 14, then proliferative from about day 15 to 28
questions.why: Estradiol builds the lining during the follicular phase, so those days are proliferative, and the progesterone that follows ovulation converts it to secretory for the second half. Reversing the two ignores that secretion requires progesterone, which is not present before ovulation. Calling the whole cycle proliferative overlooks the progesterone driven change even though estrogen is indeed present in both halves. Menstruation occupies only the first five days, not the first two weeks.
questions.answerText: Proliferative through day 14, then secretory from about day 15 to 28

questions.q: Which tissue secretes human chorionic gonadotropin in early pregnancy?
options: The anterior pituitary of the mother
The endometrial glands of the uterine lining
The corpus luteum of the ovary
questions.why: The outer trophoblast layer of the implanting embryo makes hCG, which is why the hormone appears only after implantation and why it signals that an embryo is present. The corpus luteum is the target of hCG rather than its source. The maternal anterior pituitary makes LH and FSH, and its output actually falls during pregnancy. Endometrial glands secrete nutrient fluid but not gonadotropins.

questions.q: Which receptor does human chorionic gonadotropin act on?
questions.why: Human chorionic gonadotropin is structurally close enough to LH to bind and activate the LH receptor, which is exactly how it keeps the corpus luteum alive. The FSH receptor is a different glycoprotein hormone receptor and is not the target. Progesterone receptors are intracellular steroid receptors, and hCG is a peptide that cannot use them. The oxytocin receptor belongs to a separate family on uterine and breast tissue.

questions.q: What does human chorionic gonadotropin do to the corpus luteum?
options: Causes it to involute into a corpus albicans
Converts it back into a mature follicle
Stops its progesterone output but preserves its estrogen output
Maintains it so it keeps secreting progesterone
questions.why: By occupying the LH receptor, hCG rescues the corpus luteum from its scheduled death and keeps progesterone flowing so the endometrium is not shed. Involution is exactly what hCG prevents, and it is what happens in a nonpregnant cycle. A corpus luteum cannot revert to a follicle, since luteinization is irreversible. Progesterone output is the main thing hCG sustains, so selectively stopping it reverses the hormone's purpose.
questions.answerText: Maintains it so it keeps secreting progesterone

questions.q: Around which week of pregnancy does the placenta take over progesterone production from the corpus luteum?
options: Only in the final two weeks
questions.why: The luteal placental shift happens near the end of the first trimester, which is why the corpus luteum is essential early and dispensable later. Weeks 2 to 3 is far too early, since the placenta is barely formed and hCG is only just rising. Weeks 20 to 24 is well past the point where removing the corpus luteum is safe. Waiting until the final two weeks would leave most of pregnancy dependent on a structure that cannot last that long.

questions.q: Which hormone do home pregnancy tests detect?
questions.why: Human chorionic gonadotropin is detectable in urine within days of implantation and is unique to pregnancy, which makes it the ideal test target. Progesterone is high in every luteal phase, pregnant or not, so it cannot distinguish the two. Estriol rises later in pregnancy and is not sensitive in the first weeks. Human placental lactogen also appears too late and in a pattern less specific than hCG.

questions.q: What is the main action of relaxin during pregnancy?
options: It maintains the corpus luteum after implantation
It stimulates milk synthesis in the mammary gland
It raises maternal blood glucose to feed the growing fetus
It softens the pubic ligaments, symphysis, and cervix
questions.why: Relaxin, from the corpus luteum and later the placenta, loosens pelvic connective tissue and helps ripen the cervix in preparation for delivery. Maintaining the corpus luteum is the job of hCG. Milk synthesis is driven by prolactin once the steroid block is lifted at delivery. Raising maternal glucose is largely a human placental lactogen effect, which creates insulin resistance to spare glucose for the fetus.
questions.answerText: It softens the pubic ligaments, symphysis, and cervix

questions.q: Which hormone is chiefly responsible for keeping the uterus quiet during pregnancy?
