questions.why: Progesterone suppresses myometrial excitability and holds down oxytocin receptor expression, keeping the uterus from contracting until term. Estrogen does the opposite, increasing contractility and oxytocin receptor density as term approaches. Oxytocin is the hormone that drives contractions once the uterus becomes responsive. Prostaglandins also promote contractions and cervical ripening rather than quiescence.

questions.q: Placental estrogen synthesis depends on a precursor supplied by which structure?
questions.why: The placenta lacks a key enzyme and cannot build the steroid backbone from scratch, so it relies on androgen precursor from the fetal adrenal cortex, making the two organs a single functional unit. The maternal ovary contributes little once the placenta has taken over. The fetal liver does participate by hydroxylating the precursor but is not the origin of it. The thyroid makes iodinated amine hormones and has no role in steroid supply.

questions.q: The corpus luteum is removed at week 6 of pregnancy without hormone replacement. Predict the outcome.
options: Progesterone falls but hCG rises enough to maintain the endometrium
Progesterone rises because the ovary no longer suppresses the placenta
Progesterone falls and the pregnancy is lost
Progesterone is maintained by the placenta and the pregnancy continues
questions.why: At week 6 the placenta cannot yet supply enough progesterone, so removing the corpus luteum drops progesterone and the endometrium cannot be maintained. Placental rescue is what happens after the luteal placental shift near weeks 7 to 10, not before it. Human chorionic gonadotropin works by driving the corpus luteum, so with that structure gone hCG has no target and cannot substitute. The ovary does not suppress the placenta, so removing it cannot raise progesterone.
questions.answerText: Progesterone falls and the pregnancy is lost

questions.q: The corpus luteum is removed at week 12 of pregnancy. Predict the outcome.
options: The pregnancy continues because the placenta now makes progesterone
The pregnancy is lost because progesterone falls sharply
The pregnancy continues only if hCG is given
The pregnancy continues but relaxin excess causes early labor
questions.why: By week 12 the luteal placental shift is complete, so the placenta supplies enough progesterone and the corpus luteum is no longer required. Loss of the pregnancy is the week 6 answer, and the difference between the two timings is the point of this pair. Giving hCG would not help, since there is no corpus luteum left for it to act on. Removing the corpus luteum reduces rather than increases relaxin, so relaxin excess does not follow.
questions.answerText: The pregnancy continues because the placenta now makes progesterone

questions.q: Human chorionic gonadotropin peaks near week 10 and then declines. Why does progesterone not fall along with it?
options: The corpus luteum becomes independent of any hormonal support
The maternal pituitary begins secreting LH to replace hCG
Progesterone has a half life long enough to last the pregnancy
The placenta has taken over progesterone synthesis by then
questions.why: The hCG decline is safe precisely because the placenta is now the dominant progesterone source and needs no gonadotropin to keep producing. A corpus luteum does not become self sustaining, and it involutes as hCG falls. Maternal LH is suppressed during pregnancy by high steroid levels, so the pituitary does not step in. Steroid half lives are measured in minutes to hours, so stored hormone cannot carry a pregnancy for months.
questions.answerText: The placenta has taken over progesterone synthesis by then

questions.q: Progesterone is elevated throughout pregnancy. Predict its effect on maternal ventilation and arterial PCO2.
options: Ventilation is unchanged and PCO2 falls
questions.why: Progesterone stimulates the respiratory center, so pregnant women hyperventilate mildly and arterial PCO2 settles around 30 mmHg, which also helps carbon dioxide move from fetus to mother. Reduced ventilation with a higher PCO2 would work against fetal gas exchange and is the opposite of the measured pattern. Ventilation up with PCO2 up is internally inconsistent, since more ventilation blows off carbon dioxide. Ventilation must change for PCO2 to fall, so unchanged ventilation with a low PCO2 does not follow.

questions.q: The alpha subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin is nearly identical to that of thyroid stimulating hormone. Predict the thyroid effect of very high hCG in early pregnancy.
options: Complete loss of thyroid hormone production
Mild thyroid stimulation with a slightly suppressed TSH
Mild thyroid suppression with a raised TSH
No thyroid effect, because the beta subunits differ
questions.why: At high concentrations hCG weakly cross activates the TSH receptor, nudging thyroid hormone up, and the resulting feedback lowers TSH slightly. Suppression with a raised TSH is the reverse of what a receptor agonist produces. The beta subunits do differ, which is why the effect is weak rather than strong, but weak is not zero when hCG is this abundant. Complete loss of production would require destruction of the gland, not weak stimulation of it.
questions.answerText: Mild thyroid stimulation with a slightly suppressed TSH

questions.q: Which effect of progesterone explains the heartburn and constipation common in pregnancy?
options: Increased gastric acid secretion by the stomach
Reduced blood flow to the wall of the gut
questions.why: Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle throughout the body, so the lower esophageal sphincter loosens and intestinal transit slows. Acid secretion does not rise in pregnancy, so the reflux comes from a weak sphincter rather than more acid. Increased motility would speed transit and relieve constipation rather than cause it. Gut blood flow is not reduced in pregnancy, and blood volume actually rises substantially.

questions.q: A woman conceives through in vitro fertilization after both ovaries were removed. She receives progesterone supplementation, which is stopped at week 12. Predict the outcome and explain it.
options: The pregnancy continues, because placental progesterone has replaced the missing corpus luteum
The pregnancy is lost, because without an ovary there is no progesterone source at all
The pregnancy continues only because hCG substitutes for progesterone
The pregnancy is lost, because progesterone supplementation suppressed the placenta
questions.why: Supplementation is needed only to cover the window before the luteal placental shift, and by week 12 the placenta produces enough progesterone on its own, so stopping then is safe. The ovary is not the only possible source, and that is precisely what the placenta demonstrates. Human chorionic gonadotropin is a gonadotropin, not a steroid, so it cannot substitute for progesterone in maintaining the endometrium. Exogenous progesterone does not suppress placental steroid output.
questions.answerText: The pregnancy continues, because placental progesterone has replaced the missing corpus luteum

questions.q: A fetus has a severely underdeveloped adrenal cortex. Predict maternal estriol and explain why.
options: Maternal estriol is normal, because it comes from the maternal ovary
Maternal estriol is low, because the fetal adrenal normally destroys estrogen
Maternal estriol is low, because the placenta lacks its androgen precursor
Maternal estriol is high, because the placenta compensates by making more
questions.why: The placenta cannot make the steroid backbone itself, so it depends on androgen precursor from the fetal adrenal cortex, and losing that supply drops maternal estriol. The placenta cannot compensate, because the missing step is an enzyme it does not possess. The maternal ovary is largely quiescent during pregnancy and is not the estriol source. The fetal adrenal supplies precursor rather than destroying estrogen, so the direction of that reasoning is backwards.
questions.answerText: Maternal estriol is low, because the placenta lacks its androgen precursor

questions.q: Trace the events after implantation. Which sequence correctly links human chorionic gonadotropin to the survival of the pregnancy?
options: The corpus luteum secretes hCG, the trophoblast responds, estrogen rises, the endometrium is maintained
The maternal pituitary secretes hCG, the corpus luteum responds, relaxin rises, the endometrium is maintained
Trophoblast secretes hCG, hCG binds LH receptors on the corpus luteum, progesterone stays high, the endometrium is maintained
Trophoblast secretes hCG, hCG acts on the endometrium directly, progesterone is not needed, menstruation is prevented
questions.why: The chain runs from embryo to ovary to uterus: the trophoblast makes hCG, hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive through the LH receptor, and the progesterone that results holds the secretory endometrium in place. Human chorionic gonadotropin has no direct endometrial action that could replace progesterone. The corpus luteum is the responder rather than the source, so reversing those two breaks the logic. The maternal pituitary does not make hCG, and relaxin is not what maintains the lining.
questions.answerText: Trophoblast secretes hCG, hCG binds LH receptors on the corpus luteum, progesterone stays high, the endometrium is maintained

questions.q: A pregnancy produces extremely high human chorionic gonadotropin, several times the usual peak. Which combination of findings would you expect?
options: Thyroid hormone slightly elevated, TSH slightly low, and a strongly maintained corpus luteum
Thyroid hormone slightly low, TSH slightly high, and an involuting corpus luteum
Thyroid hormone unchanged, TSH unchanged, and an involuting corpus luteum
Thyroid hormone strongly elevated, TSH strongly elevated, and a maintained corpus luteum
questions.why: Very high hCG both drives the LH receptor hard, keeping the corpus luteum robust, and weakly cross activates the TSH receptor, raising thyroid hormone enough to feed back and lower TSH. The opposite thyroid pattern would mean hCG blocked rather than stimulated the receptor. Unchanged thyroid values ignore how much cross reactivity matters at these concentrations. Thyroid hormone and TSH cannot both be strongly elevated when the feedback loop is intact, because rising thyroid hormone suppresses TSH.
questions.answerText: Thyroid hormone slightly elevated, TSH slightly low, and a strongly maintained corpus luteum

questions.q: Where is oxytocin synthesized and from where is it released?
options: Made and released entirely by the anterior pituitary
Made in the uterine wall, released into uterine veins
Made in the placenta, released into the maternal circulation
Made in the hypothalamus, released by the posterior pituitary
questions.why: Hypothalamic neurons make oxytocin and send it down their axons to nerve terminals in the posterior pituitary, where it enters the blood. The anterior pituitary makes its own hormones from glandular cells and does not store oxytocin. The uterus is a target of oxytocin, carrying receptors for it, rather than a source. The placenta makes many hormones but is not the origin of the oxytocin that drives labor.
questions.answerText: Made in the hypothalamus, released by the posterior pituitary

questions.q: Which hormone drives milk synthesis in the mammary gland?
questions.why: Prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates the alveolar cells to make milk, which is the production half of lactation. Oxytocin handles the other half, ejecting milk that has already been made. Estrogen helps the ducts develop during pregnancy but blocks actual milk production until it falls at delivery. Relaxin loosens pelvic connective tissue and has no lactogenic role.

questions.q: Which hormone causes milk ejection, sometimes called let down?
questions.why: Oxytocin contracts the myoepithelial cells wrapped around the alveoli, squeezing milk into the ducts so the infant can obtain it. Prolactin makes the milk but cannot move it, which is why the two hormones are learned as a pair. Progesterone actually blocks milk production during pregnancy and has no ejection role. Human placental lactogen prepares the breast during pregnancy but does not trigger let down.

questions.q: Which cells contract to eject milk from the alveoli?
options: Smooth muscle cells of the nipple
questions.why: Myoepithelial cells form a contractile basket around each alveolus and squeeze when oxytocin binds. Alveolar secretory cells make the milk but do not contract. Ductal epithelium lines the passageways and conducts milk rather than propelling it. There is no meaningful smooth muscle layer in the nipple that performs ejection.

questions.q: What holds prolactin secretion down when a woman is not lactating?
options: Tonic dopamine inhibition from the hypothalamus
Tonic somatostatin inhibition from the hypothalamus
Negative feedback from milk proteins in the blood
Lack of a releasing hormone from the hypothalamus
questions.why: Prolactin is unusual among anterior pituitary hormones because its default hypothalamic signal is inhibitory, and that inhibitor is dopamine. Somatostatin inhibits growth hormone and several gut hormones rather than prolactin. Milk proteins do not circulate as a feedback signal. Prolactin does not simply await a releasing hormone, which is why cutting the pituitary stalk raises prolactin while lowering every other anterior pituitary hormone.
questions.answerText: Tonic dopamine inhibition from the hypothalamus

questions.q: In the Ferguson reflex, what stimulus triggers oxytocin release during labor?
options: A rise in maternal estrogen concentration
Contraction of the abdominal wall muscles
Stretch of the cervix by the fetal head
A fall in maternal blood pressure
questions.why: Stretch receptors in the cervix fire when the fetal head presses against it, and that afferent signal reaches the hypothalamus and triggers oxytocin release. A fall in blood pressure stimulates ADH from the same posterior pituitary, but it is not the labor reflex. Estrogen prepares the uterus by raising oxytocin receptor numbers, but it is not the acute trigger for release. Abdominal muscle contraction helps in the second stage but is not the reflex stimulus.
questions.answerText: Stretch of the cervix by the fetal head

questions.q: What role do prostaglandins play in labor?
options: They suppress oxytocin release to prevent premature labor
They convert progesterone into estrogen at term
They ripen the cervix and strengthen uterine contractions
They relax the myometrium to allow fetal descent
questions.why: Prostaglandins soften the cervical connective tissue and act with oxytocin to make contractions stronger and more coordinated. Relaxation is the progesterone effect that dominates before term, not a prostaglandin effect. Prostaglandins reinforce the oxytocin loop rather than suppressing it. Steroid conversion is done by enzymes such as aromatase, not by eicosanoids.
questions.answerText: They ripen the cervix and strengthen uterine contractions

questions.q: What happens to the balance of estrogen and progesterone as term approaches?
options: Both fall sharply several weeks before labor
Both remain exactly balanced until delivery
questions.why: The shift toward estrogen raises oxytocin receptor density and gap junction formation in the myometrium, converting a quiet uterus into an excitable one. A shift toward progesterone would deepen quiescence and postpone labor. Both hormones stay high until delivery, and it is the ratio rather than an absolute fall that changes. A perfectly maintained balance would leave the uterus unable to make the transition into labor.

questions.q: Contractions push the fetal head against the cervix, cervical stretch triggers oxytocin release, and oxytocin strengthens contractions. How is this loop classified?
options: Negative feedback, because the response opposes the original stimulus
Feedforward control, because the response anticipates the stimulus
A simple reflex arc with no feedback component
Positive feedback, because the response amplifies the original stimulus
questions.why: Each turn of the loop increases the stimulus that started it, which is the definition of positive feedback and explains why labor escalates rather than settling at a steady level. Negative feedback would weaken contractions as the head descended, which would stall labor rather than complete it. Feedforward anticipates a disturbance rather than amplifying one already underway. Calling it a simple reflex misses that the output feeds back into the input.
questions.answerText: Positive feedback, because the response amplifies the original stimulus

questions.q: What ends the positive feedback loop of labor?
options: Delivery of the fetus, which removes the cervical stretch
Exhaustion of oxytocin stores in the posterior pituitary
A rise in progesterone that quiets the myometrium
questions.why: Positive feedback loops run until something removes the stimulus, and here that is birth: once the fetus is out the cervix is no longer stretched, the afferent signal stops, and oxytocin falls. Store depletion is not how the loop terminates, and oxytocin is still needed after delivery for uterine involution. Progesterone falls at this stage rather than rising. Receptor desensitization is not the mechanism, and oxytocin remains effective postpartum for controlling bleeding.
questions.answerText: Delivery of the fetus, which removes the cervical stretch

questions.q: A dopamine agonist is given to a woman shortly after delivery. Predict the effect on milk production.
options: Milk production rises, because dopamine increases oxytocin release
Milk production falls, because prolactin is suppressed
Milk production rises, because dopamine stimulates the alveolar cells
Milk production is unchanged, but let down is blocked
questions.why: Dopamine is the natural inhibitor of prolactin, so an agonist deepens that inhibition, prolactin falls, and milk synthesis stops. A rise would require dopamine to be stimulatory, which reverses its actual role at the lactotrope. Let down depends on oxytocin, which dopamine does not control, so blaming this drug for a blocked ejection reflex misassigns the target. Dopamine does not increase oxytocin release.
questions.answerText: Milk production falls, because prolactin is suppressed

questions.q: A breastfeeding woman stops nursing entirely for several days. Predict prolactin and milk volume.
options: Both prolactin and milk volume rise
Prolactin falls but milk volume is maintained
Prolactin rises but milk volume falls
Both prolactin and milk volume fall
questions.why: Suckling is the stimulus that keeps prolactin elevated, so removing it lets dopamine inhibition dominate again, prolactin falls, and production winds down. A rise in either would require continued or increased stimulation. Milk volume tracks prolactin closely, so it cannot be maintained once prolactin falls. Prolactin cannot rise without the suckling stimulus that drives it.
questions.answerText: Both prolactin and milk volume fall

questions.q: Prolactin is high throughout pregnancy, yet little milk is produced until after delivery. What explains this and what changes at birth?
options: Placental steroids block prolactin's action until the placenta is delivered
Prolactin receptors are absent until birth, and they appear within hours of delivery
Oxytocin is required for synthesis and is only released after delivery
The breast lacks alveoli until birth, and they form during the first feeding
questions.why: Placental steroids prime the breast but simultaneously block the final step of milk synthesis, so expelling the placenta drops those steroids and lets prolactin act. Prolactin receptors are present and abundant during pregnancy, which is part of how the breast is prepared. Oxytocin ejects milk rather than making it, so it cannot be the missing synthesis signal. Alveoli develop during pregnancy, well before the first feed.
questions.answerText: Placental steroids block prolactin's action until the placenta is delivered

questions.q: A woman feels uterine cramping while breastfeeding in the first days after delivery. What explains this?
options: Milk removal lowers intraabdominal pressure and stretches the uterus
Estrogen surges during feeding and stimulates contractions
Oxytocin released by suckling also contracts the myometrium
Prolactin released by suckling also contracts the myometrium
questions.why: The same oxytocin that contracts myoepithelial cells in the breast acts on uterine oxytocin receptors, which helps the uterus involute and limits bleeding. Prolactin has no contractile action on smooth muscle. Removing a modest volume of milk does not change intraabdominal pressure meaningfully. Estrogen is low in the immediate postpartum period and does not surge with feeding.
questions.answerText: Oxytocin released by suckling also contracts the myometrium

questions.q: Oxytocin is infused intravenously to a postpartum woman who is breastfeeding. Predict the effects on the uterus and on the breast.
options: Uterine contractions weaken while milk ejection increases
Neither the uterus nor the breast responds without prolactin
Uterine contractions strengthen and milk ejection increases
Uterine contractions strengthen while milk synthesis increases
questions.why: Oxytocin receptors sit on myometrium and on breast myoepithelial cells, so a systemic infusion acts on both, contracting the uterus and ejecting milk. Synthesis is a prolactin effect, so pairing oxytocin with increased milk production confuses the two halves of lactation. Oxytocin never weakens uterine contraction, and that action is why it is used to control postpartum bleeding. Both tissues respond to oxytocin directly without needing prolactin present at that moment.
questions.answerText: Uterine contractions strengthen and milk ejection increases

questions.q: A fragment of placenta is retained after delivery and continues to secrete progesterone. Predict the effect on the onset of milk production and explain it.
options: Milk production is delayed, because progesterone continues to block prolactin's action
Milk production begins early, because progesterone sensitizes the alveolar cells
Milk production is normal, because prolactin overrides any steroid effect
Milk ejection is blocked, because progesterone prevents oxytocin release
questions.why: Lactogenesis waits on the fall in placental steroids, so a source of progesterone that keeps producing after delivery holds the block in place and milk comes in late. Progesterone inhibits rather than sensitizes the final synthesis step. Prolactin cannot override the block, which is precisely why the steroid withdrawal is required. Ejection depends on oxytocin and myoepithelial cells, a pathway progesterone does not gate.
questions.answerText: Milk production is delayed, because progesterone continues to block prolactin's action

questions.q: A woman with damage to her posterior pituitary can produce milk but cannot get it out of the breast. Explain her prolactin, oxytocin, and milk supply.
options: Prolactin is deficient, oxytocin is normal, and no milk is made to eject
Both hormones are deficient, so neither production nor ejection occurs
Both hormones are normal, and the problem lies in the ducts
Prolactin is normal, oxytocin is deficient, so milk cannot be ejected
questions.why: Prolactin comes from the anterior pituitary and is unaffected, so synthesis continues, while oxytocin from the damaged posterior lobe is missing and the myoepithelial cells never contract. Deficient prolactin would mean no milk at all, which contradicts the described ability to produce it. Both hormones deficient would require damage to both lobes. Normal hormones with a duct problem would be a mechanical explanation, but the lesion given here is endocrine.
questions.answerText: Prolactin is normal, oxytocin is deficient, so milk cannot be ejected

questions.q: During labor, the fetal head is not well applied to the cervix. Predict the strength of contractions over the next hour and explain the mechanism.
options: Contractions become stronger, because oxytocin release does not depend on cervical stretch
Contractions stay weak, because less cervical stretch means less oxytocin release
Contractions become stronger, because the uterus compensates for the poor fit
Contractions stay weak, because progesterone rises to protect the fetus
questions.why: The escalation of labor depends on the loop closing: stretch to oxytocin to contraction to more stretch. Weak cervical stimulation opens the loop, so oxytocin release stays modest and contractions fail to build. There is no compensatory mechanism that strengthens contractions in the absence of the afferent signal. Progesterone is falling relative to estrogen at term and does not rise to protect the fetus. Oxytocin release in labor does depend on cervical stretch, which is the whole basis of the Ferguson reflex.
questions.answerText: Contractions stay weak, because less cervical stretch means less oxytocin release

questions.q: Explain why exclusive frequent breastfeeding tends to delay the return of ovulation after childbirth.
options: Low estrogen after delivery permanently prevents follicle recruitment
High prolactin suppresses GnRH pulses, so LH and FSH stay low and no surge occurs
High oxytocin directly destroys developing follicles in the ovary
High prolactin acts on the ovary to block estradiol receptors on granulosa cells
questions.why: Suckling keeps prolactin high, and prolactin restrains the hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator, so gonadotropins stay low, no dominant follicle matures, and the positive feedback surge never forms. Oxytocin has no follicle destroying action. Prolactin works at the hypothalamus in this setting rather than by blocking ovarian estradiol receptors. Low estrogen after delivery is temporary and does not permanently prevent recruitment, which is why cycles do return.
questions.answerText: High prolactin suppresses GnRH pulses, so LH and FSH stay low and no surge occurs

questions.q: On a standard graph of hormone levels across the menstrual cycle, which curve shows a tall narrow spike near the middle?
questions.why: The LH surge is brief and very large, so it appears as a sharp narrow spike around day 13 or 14 on a typical plot. Progesterone forms a broad rounded hill in the second half rather than a spike. FSH does show a small midcycle bump but it is much lower than the LH peak and is easy to distinguish by height. Inhibin is often not plotted at all and does not spike this way.

questions.q: On a standard cycle graph, which hormone forms a broad rounded peak near day 21?
questions.why: Progesterone climbs after ovulation as the corpus luteum matures, peaks in the mid luteal phase near day 21, and then falls, giving a wide hill rather than a spike. LH spiked a week earlier and has returned to baseline by day 21. FSH is at one of its lowest points in the mid luteal phase. Estradiol does rise again in the luteal phase but its larger and more recognizable peak is the one just before ovulation.

questions.q: How many peaks does the estradiol curve show in a normal ovulatory cycle?
options: One, in the middle of the luteal phase from the corpus luteum
Three, one in each phase of the cycle
Two, one before ovulation and a smaller luteal one
One, at the moment of ovulation
questions.why: Estradiol rises steeply as the dominant follicle matures, drops briefly at ovulation, then rises again from the corpus luteum, so the curve has two humps. A single peak at ovulation misses the luteal contribution and also misplaces the timing, since estradiol peaks just before rather than at ovulation. A single luteal peak ignores the far larger follicular rise. Three peaks does not match the two functional sources of estradiol in the cycle.
questions.answerText: Two, one before ovulation and a smaller luteal one

questions.q: On a cycle graph, what does day 1 represent?
options: The first day after bleeding stops
The day the luteinizing hormone surge begins
The first day of menstrual bleeding
questions.why: By convention the cycle is numbered from the first day of flow, which gives a landmark a person can identify without any laboratory test. Ovulation is near day 14 in a 28 day cycle, not day 1. Counting from the end of bleeding would shift every landmark by several days and make cycles hard to compare. The LH surge falls in the middle of the cycle rather than at its start.
questions.answerText: The first day of menstrual bleeding

questions.q: At which point in the cycle is follicle stimulating hormone highest on a standard graph?
options: During the first few days of the cycle
On the last day before menstruation
questions.why: FSH rises in the early follicular phase because estrogen, progesterone, and inhibin all fell when the corpus luteum died, and that rise recruits the next cohort of follicles. The mid luteal phase is when FSH is most strongly suppressed. The day before menstruation still has enough luteal steroid to hold FSH down, though it is beginning to climb. Immediately after the progesterone peak the level is still falling rather than at its maximum.
questions.answerText: During the first few days of the cycle

questions.q: On a normal cycle graph, which hormone stays flat and near zero for the entire first half of the cycle?
questions.why: There is no corpus luteum before ovulation, so progesterone has no significant source and the tracing hugs the baseline until after the surge. Estradiol rises steeply through the follicular phase and is anything but flat. FSH is actually at its highest in the first days of the cycle, then declines. Inhibin from the growing granulosa cells is present and rising through the follicular phase, which is how FSH gets pulled back down.

questions.q: On a cycle graph, ovulation is marked immediately after which feature?
questions.why: Ovulation follows the LH peak by roughly a day, so the ovulation marker sits just to the right of that spike. The progesterone peak is a consequence of ovulation and comes about a week later. The FSH nadir occurs in the luteal phase, after ovulation has already happened. Menstrual bleeding marks the start of the cycle, about two weeks before ovulation.

questions.q: On a plot of endometrial thickness across the cycle, when is the lining thinnest?
questions.why: The functionalis has just been shed during the first few days, so only the basalis remains and thickness is at its minimum. Days 12 to 14 follow a week of estrogen driven proliferation, so the lining is already thick. Days 20 to 22 show the fully developed secretory endometrium at its greatest thickness. Days 26 to 28 show the lining beginning to break down but still much thicker than immediately after shedding.

questions.q: A hormone tracing shows the luteinizing hormone peak on day 18 in a woman with regular cycles. On approximately what day should her next menstrual period begin?
questions.why: Ovulation follows the surge by about a day, and the luteal phase then runs its fixed 14 days, so counting from day 19 gives menstruation near day 32 or 33. Day 28 assumes a standard cycle rather than reading this woman's own surge. Day 25 would give a luteal phase of only about six days, shorter than the corpus luteum's lifespan. Day 36 would stretch the luteal phase past its fixed length.

questions.q: A tracing shows estradiol climbing steeply from day 8 to day 12, then a luteinizing hormone spike on day 13. What relationship do these two curves show?
options: Sustained high estradiol triggered the LH spike by positive feedback
The LH spike caused the estradiol rise that came just before it on the graph
The two curves rise independently under separate control
Falling estradiol released LH from negative feedback
questions.why: The order on the graph is the clue: estradiol is high first and for long enough, then LH spikes, which is the signature of estrogen driven positive feedback. LH cannot have caused a rise that came before it, since causes precede effects. Independent control would not explain why the spike reliably follows the estradiol peak by about a day. Estradiol is rising rather than falling in this window, so disinhibition does not fit the tracing.
questions.answerText: Sustained high estradiol triggered the LH spike by positive feedback

questions.q: A tracing covering 30 days shows normal follicular estradiol but progesterone that never rises above its baseline. What does this indicate?
options: Pregnancy occurred and hCG suppressed progesterone
The corpus luteum formed early and had already involuted
No ovulation occurred, so no corpus luteum formed
Ovulation occurred but the endometrium failed to respond
questions.why: Progesterone in a nonpregnant cycle comes almost entirely from the corpus luteum, so a flat progesterone tracing means no corpus luteum and therefore no ovulation, even though follicles clearly grew and made estradiol. Endometrial responsiveness would not change the blood level of progesterone at all. Human chorionic gonadotropin raises progesterone by rescuing the corpus luteum rather than suppressing it. An early corpus luteum would still show a progesterone rise somewhere on the tracing.
questions.answerText: No ovulation occurred, so no corpus luteum formed

questions.q: A tracing shows progesterone still climbing on day 30 rather than falling. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The next follicular cohort has started to secrete progesterone
The LH surge is about to repeat and will end the luteal phase
An embryo implanted and hCG is maintaining the corpus luteum
The corpus luteum has begun to involute more slowly than usual
questions.why: A corpus luteum has a fixed lifespan unless it is rescued, so progesterone that keeps rising past the expected end of the cycle points to hCG from an implanting embryo. Slow involution would show progesterone declining gently, not climbing. Developing follicles secrete estradiol rather than progesterone. A repeat LH surge does not occur while progesterone is high, since luteal progesterone suppresses the surge mechanism.
questions.answerText: An embryo implanted and hCG is maintaining the corpus luteum

questions.q: A tracing shows a small follicle stimulating hormone bump at midcycle, at the same time as the luteinizing hormone spike. What drives it?
options: The same sustained estradiol that drives the LH surge
The fall in progesterone that follows soon after ovulation
Inhibin released from the corpus luteum
A separate hypothalamic hormone specific to FSH
questions.why: One GnRH signal drives both gonadotropins, so the estradiol positive feedback that produces the LH surge also produces a smaller FSH rise at the same moment. Progesterone has not yet fallen at midcycle, since it has barely begun to rise. Inhibin lowers FSH rather than raising it, and the corpus luteum does not exist until after ovulation. There is no separate FSH releasing hormone, which is why the two gonadotropins move together here.
questions.answerText: The same sustained estradiol that drives the LH surge

questions.q: Two tracings are compared. One is from a 28 day cycle and one from a 35 day cycle. On which day does the luteinizing hormone peak appear in the 35 day tracing?
questions.why: Counting the fixed 14 day luteal phase back from day 35 puts ovulation near day 21 and the surge about a day earlier, near day 20. Day 14 would only be right if every cycle were 28 days, which is the error this comparison is meant to expose. Day 17 is the midpoint of a 35 day cycle, but ovulation is anchored to the end rather than the middle. Day 28 would leave only a week for the luteal phase.

questions.q: On a tracing, the estradiol peak appears about one day before the luteinizing hormone peak. What does this ordering tell you?
options: Both peaks are caused by the progesterone rise that follows them
Estradiol is the cause and the LH surge is the effect
The LH surge is the cause and the estradiol peak is the effect
The two peaks are coincidental and unrelated
questions.why: Because estradiol reaches its maximum first, and because sustained high estradiol is what switches feedback from negative to positive, the graph is showing estradiol driving the surge. Reversing the order would require the effect to precede its cause. The consistency of this one day interval across cycles rules out coincidence. Progesterone rises after both peaks, so it cannot have caused either.
questions.answerText: Estradiol is the cause and the LH surge is the effect

questions.q: A tracing shows a normal follicular estradiol rise and a clear luteinizing hormone surge, but progesterone rises only to half its usual value and is back to baseline by day 22. Interpret the tracing.
options: An embryo implanted and hCG partially rescued the corpus luteum
Ovulation occurred but the corpus luteum was inadequate and short lived
Ovulation did not occur, because progesterone never reached a normal level
The corpus luteum was normal but the assay underestimated progesterone
questions.why: A genuine LH surge with a measurable progesterone rise says ovulation happened, but a low peak that fades by day 22 says the corpus luteum is underperforming and involuting early, which shortens the luteal phase and brings menses forward. No ovulation would leave progesterone flat at baseline rather than half normal. Blaming the assay ignores that the pattern is internally consistent. An hCG rescue would sustain or raise progesterone, not let it fall early.
questions.answerText: Ovulation occurred but the corpus luteum was inadequate and short lived

questions.q: A tracing shows high luteinizing hormone and high follicle stimulating hormone across all 28 days, with estradiol flat and low and progesterone flat and low. Where is the failure?
options: In the anterior pituitary, since it cannot make enough gonadotropin to respond
In the hypothalamus, since GnRH pulses have stopped
In the endometrium, since it cannot respond to the steroids present
In the ovary, since loss of steroid and inhibin feedback frees the pituitary
questions.why: High gonadotropins with low gonadal steroids is the signature of primary gonadal failure: the ovary cannot make estradiol or inhibin, so nothing restrains the pituitary and LH and FSH climb. Pituitary failure would give low gonadotropins alongside low steroids. A hypothalamic lesion would also give low gonadotropins, so persistently high values argue strongly against it. Endometrial responsiveness affects bleeding patterns but not the circulating hormone levels being plotted.
questions.answerText: In the ovary, since loss of steroid and inhibin feedback frees the pituitary

questions.q: A tracing shows luteinizing hormone, follicle stimulating hormone, estradiol, and progesterone all flat and low for 28 days. Where is the failure?
options: In the hypothalamus or pituitary, since drive to the ovary is missing
In the ovary, since it has stopped responding to normal gonadotropin levels
In the corpus luteum, since it involutes too early each cycle
In the endometrium, since it cannot generate a feedback signal
questions.why: Everything low points upstream: without GnRH or without responsive gonadotropes, the ovary is never stimulated and makes no steroids, and there is nothing to lift the gonadotropins either. Ovarian failure would raise the gonadotropins because feedback would be lost, which is the distinguishing feature to hold onto. A short lived corpus luteum would still show a follicular estradiol rise and an LH surge. The endometrium does not send a feedback hormone to the pituitary.
questions.answerText: In the hypothalamus or pituitary, since drive to the ovary is missing

questions.q: A tracing shows estradiol rising to a moderate level around day 11, then falling, with no luteinizing hormone spike, followed by a second estradiol rise around day 22. Interpret the whole tracing.
options: Two follicles ovulated in the same cycle, one on day 12 and one on day 23
The LH surge did occur but was too brief for a daily assay to detect it
The first follicle failed to reach the surge threshold, so a new one was recruited
Ovulation occurred on day 12 and the second estradiol rise reflects a normal corpus luteum
questions.why: Positive feedback requires estradiol above a threshold and sustained for a day or two, so a moderate rise that falls away leaves the surge unformed, ovulation does not occur, and the axis recruits another follicle whose estradiol produces the second rise. Ovulation on day 12 would require an LH spike and would be followed by a progesterone rise rather than a bare estradiol rise. Two ovulations would need two surges, and the tracing shows none. Calling the surge undetectable ignores that a surge lasts many hours and would appear on a daily sampling protocol.
questions.answerText: The first follicle failed to reach the surge threshold, so a new one was recruited
